28bc72c9.subtitle: Answers to common questions from your OB/GYN team at Women's Specialists of Clear Lake

subsections.title: When should I schedule my first visit?
subsections.body: Schedule as soon as pregnancy is confirmed — ideally between 8–10 weeks. We'll confirm the pregnancy, estimated due date, and start your care plan.

subsections.title: How often will I be seen?
subsections.body: Monthly until 28 weeks · every 2 weeks 28–36 weeks · weekly 36–40 weeks · twice weekly after 40 weeks.

subsections.title: What prenatal vitamins should I take?
subsections.body: Begin a prenatal vitamin with at least 400–800 mcg of folic acid as soon as possible. Start before conception if planning a pregnancy.

subsections.title: How much extra should I eat?
subsections.body: Extra calorie needs: 0 extra in 1st trimester · ~340/day 2nd · ~450/day 3rd trimester. Focus on nutrient quality, not just quantity.

subsections.title: What medications are safe?
subsections.body: Generally safe: Tylenol (acetaminophen), Tums, Zofran (with approval), prenatal vitamins. Avoid NSAIDs (ibuprofen, Advil) especially after 20 weeks.

subsections.title: Can I exercise?
subsections.body: Yes! 30 minutes of moderate exercise most days is recommended unless complications arise. Walking, swimming, and prenatal yoga are excellent choices.

subsections.title: Can I travel?
subsections.body: Generally safe until 36 weeks. Avoid long trips after 28 weeks without medical clearance. Stay hydrated and move frequently on long trips.

subsections.title: 8–10 weeks
subsections.body: Confirm pregnancy, EDD, baseline labs, genetic counseling

subsections.title: 11–14 weeks
subsections.body: First trimester screen, NT ultrasound, NIPT if desired

subsections.title: 16–18 weeks
subsections.body: Quad screen, hear heartbeat, discuss anatomy scan

subsections.title: 18–22 weeks
subsections.body: Anatomy ultrasound — detailed fetal survey

subsections.title: 24–28 weeks
subsections.body: Gestational diabetes screen (1-hr glucose), Tdap

subsections.title: 28–36 weeks
subsections.body: Every 2 weeks; RhoGAM if Rh-negative

subsections.title: 36–40 weeks
subsections.body: Weekly; GBS swab; birth plan discussion

subsections.title: 40+ weeks
subsections.body: Twice weekly; NST; discuss induction options

subsections.title: Call us immediately / Go to L&D
items: Signs of preeclampsia: severe headache, vision changes, swelling in face/hands

subsections.title: After-hours emergency
subsections.body: Call our office or go directly to Clear Lake Regional Medical Center L&D

subsections.title: Recommended & safe
items: Flu vaccine: Every flu season (any trimester)
COVID-19: Recommended; discuss with Dr. Klein

RSV (Abrysvo): one dose at 32 weeks 0 days–36 weeks 6 days, September–January. If you received a maternal RSV vaccine in a previous pregnancy, CDC does not recommend another dose; ask about infant RSV immunization instead.

subsections.title: Avoid live vaccines in pregnancy
subsections.body: MMR, Varicella, Live flu mist, Yellow fever

subsections.title: Protecting you and your newborn
subsections.body: Vaccines are the safest way to protect you and your newborn from serious illness.

sections.title: Questions? We're here for you 24/7
sections.body: No question is too small. Call our office at (281) 557-0300 during office hours. For after-hours emergencies, leave a message and our on-call provider will return your call. We're honored to be part of your pregnancy journey.

7d319ac9.intro: Congratulations on your pregnancy. Most symptoms in pregnancy are normal and related to hormonal and physical changes. However, some symptoms can be warning signs of a serious condition. Please contact our office or seek urgent care immediately if you experience any of the following:

sections.title: Call 911 or go to the ER immediately
items: Shortness of breath at rest or difficulty breathing
Thoughts of harming yourself or others
Heavy vaginal bleeding (soaking 1 pad/hour or large clots)

subsections.title: Bleeding or fluid concerns
items: Gush or steady leakage of fluid from the vagina

subsections.title: Pain
items: Severe cramping not relieved by rest
Persistent right upper abdominal pain (under ribs)
Severe back pain with pelvic pressure

subsections.title: Headache or vision changes
items: Severe headache not improved with rest or Tylenol
Blurred vision, flashing lights, or temporary vision loss
Sudden swelling of face, hands, or around eyes

subsections.title: Blood pressure / Preeclampsia symptoms
items: Feeling generally unwell in second half of pregnancy

subsections.title: Fever or infection
items: Persistent cough with shortness of breath

subsections.title: Decreased baby movement (after 28 weeks)
subsections.body: Movement should not decrease toward the end of pregnancy.
items: Noticeable decrease in baby’s usual movement pattern
Fewer than 10 movements in 2 hours during active time

sections.title: Mental health matters
items: Trouble sleeping unrelated to pregnancy discomfort
Feeling overwhelmed or unable to cope

sections.title: Common symptoms that are usually normal
sections.body: Still call if severe or concerning to you.
items: Mild shortness of breath with activity
Braxton Hicks contractions (irregular, not painful, resolve with rest)

sections.title: Trust your instincts
sections.body: If something feels wrong, call. You know your body best. If you are unsure whether a symptom is serious, it is always appropriate to contact our office for guidance.

14a92cf3.title: Vaccines & pregnancy
14a92cf3.subtitle: Protecting you and your baby — before, during, and after pregnancy
14a92cf3.intro: When you get vaccinated, you aren't just protecting yourself — your body makes antibodies that cross the placenta and give your baby early protection during the first months of life, before they are old enough for their own vaccines. Some vaccines are best given before pregnancy, others are given during pregnancy according to vaccine history and seasonal eligibility, and a few are given after delivery to catch up.

subsections.title: The best time to get fully protected is before you conceive
items: We check your immunity to measles, rubella & chickenpox (varicella)
MMR and varicella are live vaccines — get them, then wait 4 weeks before trying to conceive
Flu shot any time you may become pregnant
Catch up on HPV vaccine through age 26
Hepatitis A & B and pneumococcal if you have risk factors
A preconception visit is the ideal time to review your vaccine history

sections.title: During pregnancy — vaccine timing and eligibility

subsections.title: Tdap · 27–36 weeks · Every pregnancy
subsections.body: Protects against tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis (whooping cough). Whooping cough is especially dangerous for newborns — it can cause them to stop breathing and turn blue. Getting Tdap in the third trimester lets your antibodies cross the placenta and protect your baby from birth until their own vaccine at 2 months.

subsections.title: Flu (Influenza) · Any trimester · Flu season
subsections.body: Pregnancy changes your immune, heart, and lung function, making you much more likely to become seriously ill from the flu. The flu also raises the risk of premature labor. The shot passes antibodies to your baby, protecting them before their own vaccine at 6 months.
items: Get it by end of October if possible
Flu shot only — not the nasal spray

subsections.title: RSV (Abrysvo) · 32 weeks 0 days–36 weeks 6 days · September–January
subsections.body: RSV is the leading cause of infant hospitalization in the U.S. The Pfizer vaccine (Abrysvo) is the only RSV vaccine approved in pregnancy. Antibodies pass to your baby and protect against severe RSV for their first 6 months. If you don't get the RSV vaccine, your baby can instead receive an antibody shot (nirsevimab) after birth.
items: One dose at 32 weeks 0 days through 36 weeks 6 days
September through January in this area
If you received a maternal RSV vaccine in any previous pregnancy, CDC does not recommend another dose in a subsequent pregnancy. Ask your care team about infant RSV immunization instead.
Helps protect your baby during the first months of life

subsections.title: 1st trimester
subsections.body: Flu shot if season is active

subsections.title: 2nd trimester
subsections.body: Flu shot if season is active

subsections.title: 3rd trimester · 27–36 weeks
subsections.body: Tdap every pregnancy

subsections.title: 3rd trimester · 32–36 weeks
subsections.body: RSV (Abrysvo) Sept–Jan only

subsections.title: Flu season (any trimester)
subsections.body: Flu shot by end of October

subsections.title: Catch up on anything you couldn't get during pregnancy
items: If you were non-immune to measles, rubella, or chickenpox, get those vaccines now
These live vaccines are safe while breastfeeding
Start or finish the HPV series if you're age 26 or younger
Catch up on any Hepatitis A/B or pneumococcal doses you still need

sections.title: Vaccines to avoid during pregnancy
items: Live vaccines are not given while pregnant: MMR, varicella (chickenpox), and the nasal-spray flu (FluMist) — get these before or after pregnancy
It's perfectly fine for your family members to receive these live vaccines
If a live vaccine is given before a pregnancy is known, don't worry — no fetal harm has ever been reported

sections.title: Are these vaccines safe?
sections.body: Yes. The flu shot, Tdap, and RSV vaccine are studied extensively in pregnancy and recommended by ACOG, the CDC, and the AAP. The vaccines given during pregnancy are not live and cannot give you the disease. Side effects are mild and temporary — arm soreness, low-grade fever, or fatigue for 1–2 days — signs your immune system is responding. Vaccines do not cause autism or infertility.

sections.title: Questions about vaccines?
sections.body: Talk to us at your next visit. We're happy to review your vaccination history and make sure you and your baby are fully protected — before, during, and after pregnancy. No question is too small. You can also find reliable information at cdc.gov/vaccines.

W E L C O M E

Congratulations on your pregnancy. Whether this is your first baby or your fifth, we are honored that you've chosen us to care for you. Pregnancy is a remarkable time, and our goal is to make it feel calm, informed, and well-supported from your very first visit through the weeks after delivery.

This packet is yours to keep. It explains what we'll check at each visit, the screening tests we offer and when, the symptoms that should prompt a call to the office, and clear, evidence-based answers to the questions patients most commonly ask. Think of it as a companion — flip to a section when something comes up rather than reading it cover to cover.

The recommendations here reflect current guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) and the CDC. Some details — particularly around timing of tests, aspirin for preeclampsia prevention, and the vaccines now recommended in pregnancy — have been updated to reflect 2026 standards of care.

A few things we want you to know now: call us anytime you are worried. There is no question too small, and we would always rather hear from you than have you wait. Keep this packet handy, bring your questions to every visit, and lean on us when you need to.
With warmth, Sarah Quintero, RN — and the team at Women's Specialists of Clear Lake Registered Nurse · 281-557-0300 ext. 24876

rows: Confirmation, dating ultrasound, full prenatal labs BLOODWORK Complete blood count, blood type and Rh, antibody screen, rubella, varicella, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B and C, TSH, urine culture, chlamydia and gonorrhea, Pap if due. Expanded carrier screening is offered to every patient.

blocks.text: Call us right away if… You know your body best. When in doubt, call. The main line — 281-557-0300 — connects to the on-call physician day or night.
Vaginal bleeding
Any bright red bleeding, or spotting that soaks a pad, at any point in pregnancy.
Severe or persistent headache
Especially with visual changes, swelling, or right- upper-abdominal pain — can be a sign of preeclampsia.
Decreased fetal movement
Fewer than 10 movements in an hour after a meal, or a clear change from the baby's usual pattern after 28 weeks.
Fluid leaking
A gush or steady trickle of fluid from the vagina at any stage.
Regular painful contractions
Before 37 weeks, or coming every 5 minutes for an hour at term.

Especially with chills, urinary symptoms, or upper- abdominal pain.
Sudden swelling
Marked swelling in the face, hands, or one leg — particularly with calf pain or shortness of breath.

Constant, severe, or one-sided pain that doesn't ease with rest.

Unable to keep anything down for more than 24 hours, or feeling weak and dizzy.

Persistent sadness, anxiety, intrusive thoughts, or thoughts of harming yourself or the baby — at any point during or after pregnancy.

Pregnancy basics &
testing
FA Q · PA R T 1 O F 4
Quick, evidence-based answers to questions about prenatal care, due dates, and the screenings we offer along the way.

What is prenatal care? The series of checkups and tests during pregnancy that monitor your health and the baby's growth and catch issues early. Consistent prenatal care is one of the single most important things you can do for a healthy pregnancy.

How is my due date set? Forty weeks from the first day of your last period, typically confirmed by a first-trimester ultrasound. The ultrasound estimate replaces the period-based one if they differ by more than 5–7 days early in pregnancy.
What is a fetal heartbeat? The sound of the baby's heart, usually audible by Doppler around 10–12 weeks. Normal rate is 110–160 beats per minute.

What is an ultrasound? A safe, non-invasive imaging test that uses sound waves to look at the baby. You'll have a first-trimester dating scan in our office, a detailed anatomy scan at 18–22 weeks, and a growth scan around 30–34 weeks. Extra scans may be added if clinically indicated.

What is NIPT? Non-invasive prenatal testing is a blood draw from you that screens for Down syndrome, trisomy 13 and 18, and certain sex- chromosome conditions. It can also reveal the baby's sex. ACOG now recommends offering it to all pregnant patients starting at 10 weeks, regardless of age.

What is carrier screening? A blood test that shows whether you (and if needed, your partner) carry a recessive gene for conditions like cystic fibrosis, spinal muscular atrophy, or sickle cell. We now offer expanded carrier screening — a single panel covering hundreds of conditions — to every patient.

What is amniocentesis? A diagnostic test performed between 15 and 20 weeks in which a small sample of amniotic fluid is taken to test the baby's chromosomes. Considered when screening is abnormal or risk is elevated.

What is gestational diabetes? Diabetes that develops during pregnancy when the body can't keep up with insulin demand. Untreated, it raises the risk of a large baby, cesarean, and birth complications. We screen every patient between 24 and 28 weeks, earlier if risk factors are present.

What is Group B strep? A common bacterium that lives harmlessly in many adults but can cause serious infection in newborns. We swab the vagina and rectum between 36 0⁄7 and 37 6⁄7 weeks. If positive, you'll get IV antibiotics during labor — highly effective at protecting the baby.

What is a fetal non-stress test? A 20–40 minute check in the third trimester where two belts on your abdomen record the baby's heart rate and any contractions. Used when there are concerns about movement, growth, blood pressure, or diabetes.

What is a high-risk pregnancy? A pregnancy with an increased chance of complications because of your age, medical conditions (hypertension, diabetes, autoimmune disease), prior pregnancy history, or how this pregnancy is developing. High-risk pregnancies get more frequent monitoring and sometimes co-management with a maternal-fetal medicine specialist.

What is advanced maternal age? Delivery at 35 or older. There is a modestly higher risk of gestational diabetes, hypertension, preterm birth, and chromosomal differences. With good prenatal care, most pregnancies at this age go well.

What is a doula? A trained non-medical professional who provides physical, emotional, and informational support during labor and the postpartum period. Doulas don't replace your medical team — they complement it. Many patients find their presence reassuring.

What is a childbirth education class? A short course covering the stages of labor, comfort and pain options, breastfeeding, and newborn basics. Many local hospitals offer them — ask us for recommendations.

Eating, moving & daily
life
FA Q · PA R T 2 O F 4
Practical, evidence-based guidance on nutrition, exercise, work, and the everyday questions that come up between visits.

What is a prenatal vitamin? A daily multivitamin formulated for pregnancy. The key ingredients are folic acid (at least 400 mcg, 600 mcg ideal), iron, iodine, choline, and DHA. Start before conception if you can, and continue through breastfeeding.

How much water should I drink? About 8–12 cups (64–96 oz) of fluid daily, sipped throughout the day. Pale yellow urine is a good sign you're hydrated. Add electrolytes if you're vomiting or sweating heavily.

Can I exercise during my pregnancy? Yes — and you should. Aim for 150 minutes a week of moderate activity (brisk walking, swimming, stationary cycling, prenatal yoga). Avoid contact sports, high fall-risk activities, and exercise lying flat on your back after the first trimester. Stop and call us if you have bleeding, fluid leakage, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or contractions.

Can I continue to work? Most jobs are safe throughout pregnancy. Talk to us if your work involves heavy lifting, prolonged standing, chemical exposure, or significant fall risk so we can advise on modifications.

Can I travel during pregnancy? Generally yes, with sensible precautions. Stand and walk every 1–2 hours on long trips to reduce blood clot risk, and stay well hydrated. Most airlines allow flying up to 36 weeks. Stay close to home after 34 weeks. Check destination Zika and other travel advisories before booking.

What foods should I avoid? Raw or undercooked meat, poultry, eggs, or seafood Unpasteurized dairy, juice, or soft cheeses (feta, brie, queso fresco) unless labeled pasteurized Cold deli meats and hot dogs unless heated to steaming High-mercury fish: shark, swordfish, king mackerel, tilefish, bigeye tuna, marlin, orange roughy More than 200 mg caffeine per day (~one 12 oz brewed coffee) Any alcohol
What about fish? Low-mercury fish are encouraged — aim for 2–3 servings (8–12 oz) per week. Best choices include salmon, sardines, anchovies, shrimp, cod, tilapia, and canned light tuna.

How much weight should I gain? Targets are based on your starting BMI — see the weight gain page near the back of this packet. Slow and steady gain in the 2nd and 3rd trimester is the goal, not a number on a single visit.

What medications are safe? Always confirm with us, but commonly used options include: Pain/fever: Tylenol (acetaminophen). Avoid ibuprofen and other NSAIDs after 20 weeks. Cold/allergies: Saline nasal spray, Claritin, Zyrtec, Benadryl, plain Tylenol Cold Cough: Plain Robitussin, Dimetapp Heartburn: Tums, Pepcid, Prilosec, Nexium Constipation: Miralax, Colace, Metamucil, Fibercon Diarrhea: Imodium AD; BRAT diet — call us if >24 hr Hemorrhoids: Preparation H, Tucks pads, Anusol Nausea: Vitamin B6, ginger, Unisom, Sea Bands Leg cramps: Hydration, magnesium-rich foods

Which vaccines are recommended? Tdap — every pregnancy, 27–36 weeks (protects baby from whooping cough) RSV (Abrysvo) — 32 weeks 0 days–36 weeks 6 days during September–January; no repeat maternal dose after vaccination in a previous pregnancy. Ask about infant RSV immunization instead. Flu — any trimester during flu season COVID-19 — per current CDC guidance Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) are not given in pregnancy — get them postpartum if needed.

What should I bring to each visit? Your insurance card, a current medication list (including supplements), recent records or imaging from outside providers, and any questions you've collected between visits.

Common symptoms & what
helps
FA Q · PA R T 3 O F 4
Pregnancy comes with a long list of unfamiliar sensations. Most are normal — here's how to recognize and manage the most common ones, and when to call.

Morning sickness Common in the first trimester, usually improves by week 12–14. Try small frequent meals, ginger or B6, Unisom (doxylamine) at night, and Sea Bands. Call if you can't keep fluids down for 24 hours, lose weight, or feel weak.

Back pain Driven by posture changes and the growing uterus. Heat or cold, supportive shoes, a maternity belt, prenatal yoga, side-sleeping with a pillow between the knees, and gentle stretching all help. Chiropractic care or physical therapy are reasonable if symptoms persist.
Round ligament pain Sharp, brief pains in the lower belly or groin from the round ligaments stretching. Move slowly between positions, apply heat, and use a support belt.
Pelvic pressure late in pregnancy From the baby's head settling into the pelvis. A support belt, side- lying rest, warm baths, and pelvic floor exercises all help.

Symphysis pubis pain Pain over the pubic bone or hips from softening pelvic ligaments. Avoid wide stances when getting out of bed or a car (keep knees together), use a support belt, and ask about pelvic floor physical therapy.
Constipation Increase fluids to 8–10 cups daily, add fiber (fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes), keep moving, and use Colace 100 mg 1– 2 times a day or Miralax as needed.

Shortness of breath Normal late in pregnancy as the uterus crowds the diaphragm. Sit upright, take slow deep breaths, sleep with extra pillows. Call us for sudden severe breathlessness, chest pain, calf pain, or coughing up blood — those need urgent evaluation.

Dizziness From blood volume shifts and the uterus pressing on blood vessels. Stand up slowly, stay hydrated, eat regularly, avoid lying flat on your back, wear compression stockings, and sleep on your left side.

Numb hands Carpal tunnel of pregnancy is common — fluid presses on the median nerve. A wrist splint worn at night, gentle stretching, and avoiding repetitive wrist motion usually help. Most cases resolve postpartum.

Nosebleeds From increased blood flow and more fragile nasal vessels. Saline spray, a little petroleum jelly inside the nostrils, and gentle blowing help. Pinch closed for 10 minutes if bleeding. Go to the ER if bleeding persists or you feel faint.

PUPPS rash Itchy, red bumps usually starting on the abdomen in the third trimester. Try cool baths, fragrance-free moisturizers, calamine, hydrocortisone cream, and loose cotton clothing. Severe or generalized itching — especially on palms and soles — needs to be checked for cholestasis.

Bleeding in early pregnancy Light spotting can be normal (implantation, after intercourse, post- exam). Call us for any bleeding so we can decide whether to evaluate. Heavier bleeding with pain may indicate miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy — go to the ER if you can't reach us.

What are kick counts? Starting around 28 weeks, lie on your side after a meal and time how long it takes to feel 10 movements. Most babies do this in under an hour. Repeat 2–3 times a week. Call us if it takes longer or your baby's pattern feels different.

Conditions, labor &
postpartum
FA Q · PA R T 4 O F 4
A reference for some of the conditions and decisions that may come up later in pregnancy — and what to expect once your baby arrives.

What is preeclampsia? High blood pressure with signs of organ involvement (typically protein in the urine), most often after 20 weeks. Risk factors include first pregnancy, age 35+, BMI >30, multiples, chronic hypertension, diabetes, and kidney or autoimmune disease. We start 81 mg aspirin daily before 16 weeks for patients at increased risk to lower it.

What is cholestasis of pregnancy? A liver condition causing intense itching (often palms and soles), sometimes with darker urine or jaundice. It requires monitoring and earlier delivery to protect the baby. Tell us promptly if you're itching badly.
What is placenta previa? The placenta covers part or all of the cervix. It often resolves as the uterus grows; if it persists, delivery is by cesarean. Bleeding from previa needs urgent evaluation.

What is preterm labor? Labor before 37 weeks. Symptoms include regular contractions, low back pain, pelvic pressure, vaginal bleeding, or fluid leaking. Call immediately — there are treatments to slow labor and protect the baby's lungs if delivery is imminent.

What if I'm Rh-negative? If your blood type is Rh-negative and the baby may be Rh- positive, your immune system can produce antibodies that attack the baby's blood cells in this or a future pregnancy. We prevent that with RhoGAM, an injection given around 28 weeks and again after delivery if the baby is Rh-positive.

What if my baby is breech? Around 37 weeks, if the baby is bottom- or feet-first, we can offer an external cephalic version — a procedure to gently turn the baby head-down. If that's not successful or appropriate, delivery is by cesarean.

What are the signs of labor? Regular, strengthening contractions (every 5 minutes for an hour at term), low back pain, a "bloody show," or your water breaking. Call us — we'll talk through whether to head to the hospital.

How is labor induced? If induction is recommended (post-dates, hypertension, growth concerns, etc.), methods include cervical ripening (Cervidil or Misoprostol), a Foley balloon, oxytocin (Pitocin), and/or rupturing the membranes. The mix depends on how favorable your cervix is.

What is a cesarean delivery? A surgical delivery through an incision in the lower abdomen, planned or unplanned. We perform a C-section when it's the safest option for you or the baby — for example, with a previa, certain breech positions, or fetal distress in labor.

What about VBAC? A trial of labor after a prior cesarean is reasonable for many patients. We'll review your prior records and discuss the risks and benefits, and you'll sign a consent if you choose this path.

What is postpartum hemorrhage? Heavier-than-expected bleeding after delivery, usually because the uterus doesn't contract well. Risk factors include cesarean, large baby, or prolonged labor. It's managed in the hospital, and your team watches closely.

What is postpartum care? Care doesn't end at delivery. ACOG now recommends an early visit within 3 weeks, with a comprehensive visit by 12 weeks. We check on your recovery, mood, breastfeeding, contraception, and any conditions that arose in pregnancy.

What is postpartum depression? Sadness, anxiety, irritability, or intrusive thoughts that don't lift after a couple of weeks, or that interfere with daily life. It affects roughly 1 in 7 birthing parents and is very treatable. We screen at every postpartum visit — and you can call any time.

What is a lactation consultant? A trained professional (often an IBCLC) who helps with positioning, supply, and any breastfeeding problem. Most hospitals offer one before discharge, and we can refer you to an outpatient consultant.
What is a newborn screening test? A heel-stick blood test in the first day or two of life that screens for dozens of treatable conditions — hypothyroidism, sickle cell, PKU, and more.

About circumcision & cord blood Circumcision is a personal decision. Benefits include slightly reduced UTIs in infancy, easier hygiene, and reduced HIV/HPV transmission later; risks (bleeding, infection) are uncommon. Cord blood can be donated to a public bank or stored privately for your family. Public donation is free; private banking carries an ongoing cost with a low likelihood of use. Q: Do I need to gain less weight if I'm obese?
Yes — ACOG recommends only 11–20 lbs total for women with BMI ≥30. Some women with severe obesity may safely gain less or none with physician supervision.
Q: Are weight loss medications safe in pregnancy?
No. All anti-obesity medications (GLP-1 agonists, phentermine, etc.) should be stopped before conception or immediately upon discovering pregnancy.

pregnancy?
Gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, C-section, preterm birth, and macrosomia (large baby). These are monitored closely throughout your care.
Q: When can I restart weight management after
delivery?
Usually 6 weeks postpartum for diet/exercise. If breastfeeding, medication decisions are made individually. Dr. Klein will create a postpartum plan.

🤢Morning Sickness & Nausea
Managing nausea and vomiting during pregnancy — from mild discomfort to hyperemesis
WHAT IS IT & WHY DOES IT HAPPEN?

Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (NVP) affects 70–80% of pregnant women. Despite the name, "morning sickness" can occur any time of day. Rising hCG levels and estrogen are the main triggers. Symptoms typically begin at 4–6 weeks and peak at 8–10 weeks. Most women improve by 16 weeks.
SEVERITY SCALE
Mild Nausea without vomiting, manages daily activities
Moderate Nausea + occasional vomiting, some impact on life
Severe Frequent vomiting, weight loss, dehydration
Hyperemesis Gravidarum — vomiting >3×/day, >5% weight loss, hospitalization may be needed
DIET & LIFESTYLE TIPS
Eat small, frequent meals (every 1.5–2 hrs)
Eat crackers or dry toast before getting out of bed
Avoid an empty stomach — keep snacks nearby
Cold foods often better tolerated (less smell)
Avoid greasy, spicy, or strong-smelling foods
Stay upright 30–60 min after eating
Ginger tea, ginger ale, ginger chews ✓ Safe
Acupressure wristbands (Sea-Bands) ✓ Safe
HYDRATION STRATEGY
Sip fluids slowly and frequently — not large gulps
Try ice chips or popsicles if drinking is difficult
Lemon water, diluted juice, or sports drinks
Electrolyte drinks (Pedialyte, Gatorade) OTC
Avoid carbonated drinks if they worsen symptoms
Cold, clear beverages often better tolerated
Urine should be pale yellow — dark = dehydrated
OTC & SUPPLEMENT OPTIONS
Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) 10–25 mg TID OTC
Unisom (doxylamine) — used with B6 OTC
Diclegis/Bonjesta = B6 + doxylamine combined RX
Ginger supplements 250 mg QID OTC
Switch prenatal vitamin to evening dose; try gummies formulation
PRESCRIPTION MEDICATIONS
Ondansetron (Zofran) — very effective, widely used RX
Promethazine — older antiemetic, sedating RX
Metoclopramide (Reglan)
RX
Prochlorperazine (Compazine)
RX
IV fluids + thiamine — for hyperemesis gravidarum
Methylprednisolone — refractory HG only
⚠ CALL YOUR DOCTOR IF YOU HAVE
Vomiting more than 3–4 times per day
Signs of dehydration: dark urine, dizziness, dry mouth
Blood in vomit or severe abdominal pain
Fever with vomiting
Unable to keep any fluids down for 24 hours
Weight loss of more than 5 lbs
Nausea starting suddenly after 10 weeks
No improvement despite OTC measures

💚 Nausea Can Actually Be a Good Sign! Studies show women with nausea in early pregnancy have a lower risk of miscarriage. It is your body responding to the rapid hormonal changes of early pregnancy. This phase will pass — most women feel dramatically better by the second trimester. Hang in there; relief is coming!

🦴Back Pain in Pregnancy
Understanding, managing, and relieving pregnancy-related back pain
WHAT IS IT & WHY IT HAPPENS

Back pain affects up to 70% of pregnant women. As your uterus grows, your center of gravity shifts forward, placing increased strain on back muscles. Hormones like relaxin loosen ligaments and joints to prepare for delivery — but also reduce spinal stability.
WHO IS AT RISK
Prior history of back pain or injury
Multiple pregnancy (twins, triplets)
Jobs requiring prolonged standing or lifting
Weak core/abdominal muscles
BMI >25 before pregnancy
Second or subsequent pregnancies
SYMPTOMS & TYPES
Lumbar pain — lower back ache, worse with activity
Posterior pelvic pain — deep buttock/hip pain
Sciatica — radiating pain down the leg
Round ligament pain — sharp sides-of-belly pain
Typically worse in second and third trimesters
Often worse at end of day or after prolonged sitting
SAFE TREATMENTS
✓ Prenatal yoga and gentle stretching
✓ Warm (not hot) compresses — 20 min max
✓ Pregnancy support belt or belly band
✓ Physical therapy / chiropractic care
✓ Acetaminophen (Tylenol) OTC
✗ Ibuprofen / NSAIDs — avoid in pregnancy
POSTURE & ERGONOMICS
Sleep on your left side with a pillow between knees
Avoid high heels — wear supportive flat shoes
Bend at the knees when lifting; avoid twisting
Sit in chairs with good lumbar support
Use a footrest to raise legs when seated
Avoid standing for long periods without breaks
EXERCISE & STRENGTHENING
Pelvic tilts — flatten low back against floor
Cat-cow stretches on hands and knees
Swimming or water aerobics — excellent low-impact
Walking with proper posture — 20–30 min/day
Kegel exercises to strengthen pelvic floor
Prenatal Pilates with certified instructor
⚠ WHEN TO CALL YOUR DOCTOR IMMEDIATELY
Severe or sudden-onset back pain
Pain radiating down both legs
Loss of bladder or bowel control
Regular cramping or uterine tightening with back pain
Back pain with fever or chills (kidney infection?)
Numbness, tingling, or weakness in legs
Back pain with vaginal bleeding
Pain unrelieved by rest or Tylenol

💚 You've Got This! Back pain in pregnancy is very common and almost always temporary — it typically resolves within a few months after delivery. Most women find relief with gentle exercise, good posture, and support. Your care team is here to help you stay comfortable throughout your pregnancy journey.

🤲 Carpal Tunnel Syndrome During Pregnancy
Numbness and tingling in the hands is common in pregnancy — and there is a lot we can do about it
WHAT IS CARPAL TUNNEL SYNDROME?
•It happens when a nerve in the wrist — the median nerve — is squeezed
•During pregnancy, normal fluid retention and swelling place extra pressure on this nerve
•It is common, especially later in pregnancy
•It can affect one or both hands
COMMON SYMPTOMS
•Tingling, "pins and needles," burning, or numbness in the thumb, index,
middle, and part of the ring finger
•Symptoms that are worse at night or that wake you from sleep
•Hand or wrist pain
•Swelling or stiffness in the hands
•Weak grip, clumsiness, or dropping objects
WEAR A WRIST SPLINT AT NIGHT
✓ A splint that holds your wrist straight or neutral reduces pressure on the nerve
✓ Wear it while sleeping — this is the single most helpful step for most patients
✓ If symptoms bother you during the day, we may suggest wearing it for certain activities too
✓ Splints are available over the counter; ask us if you are unsure which to buy
ADJUST YOUR ACTIVITIES
✓ Take frequent breaks from repeated gripping or wrist bending
✓ Keep your wrist as straight as possible with a phone, keyboard, or steering wheel
✓ Avoid sleeping with your wrists bent under your body or pillow
✓ Change positions often during repetitive hand tasks
REDUCE SWELLING
✓ Rest with your hands elevated on pillows when you can
✓ Gently open and close your hands several times through the day
✓ Follow your pregnancy care plan for healthy activity, hydration, and nutrition
WILL IT GO AWAY?
•For many patients, symptoms improve after delivery as pregnancy swelling goes down
•Symptoms can sometimes continue after pregnancy
•Please mention any ongoing numbness, tingling, pain, or weakness at your
postpartum visit
•We can still treat it after delivery — do not assume you have to live with it
IF CONSERVATIVE MEASURES ARE NOT ENOUGH
•Additional options such as hand therapy or a steroid injection may be considered when symptoms are significant or do not improve
•Important: do not start a new medication, supplement, or treatment for hand or wrist pain during pregnancy without discussing it with your obstetric care team first
⚠ CONTACT OUR OFFICE IF
⚠ Symptoms are severe, constant, or worsening
⚠ You are frequently dropping objects or struggling with daily activities
⚠ Symptoms continue after delivery
⚠ You have weakness in your thumb or hand
⚠ A wrist splint and activity changes are not helping
⚠ You develop sudden swelling of the face or hands, a bad headache, or vision changes
💚 Simple Steps Help — Start With a Night Splint

Carpal tunnel symptoms in pregnancy can be genuinely miserable, especially when they keep waking you at night. The good news is that simple steps — most of all a night splint — help many patients, and symptoms often ease after delivery. Please tell us if your hands are bothering you, even if it seems minor.

blocks.text: Dizziness in Pregnancy
Patient Education Pamphlet
Is Dizziness Common in Pregnancy?
Yes. Many women experience dizziness at some point during pregnancy. It can feel like:
Lightheadedness
Feeling faint
Room spinning (vertigo)
Unsteadiness
Most causes are normal and related to pregnancy changes, but occasionally dizziness can signal a more serious condition.
Common Causes
1. Low Blood Pressure — Hormonal changes cause blood vessels to relax, which may lower blood pressure—especially in the
first and second trimesters.
2. Lying Flat on Your Back — In later pregnancy, the uterus can press on major blood vessels when you lie on your back,
reducing blood flow and causing dizziness (supine hypotensive syndrome).
3. Low Blood Sugar — Skipping meals or long gaps between eating can cause lightheadedness.
4. Dehydration — Not drinking enough fluids can worsen dizziness.
5. Anemia — Low iron levels are common in pregnancy and may cause fatigue and dizziness.
6. Sudden Position Changes — Standing up too quickly can cause a brief drop in blood pressure (orthostatic hypotension).
What You Can Do
Helpful Tips
Change positions slowly, especially when getting out of bed.
Avoid lying flat on your back after the first trimester; lie on your side instead (preferably left side).
Eat small, frequent meals to keep blood sugar stable.
Stay well hydrated (aim for 8–12 cups of fluids daily unless otherwise instructed).
Take prescribed prenatal vitamins and iron as directed.
Sit or lie down immediately if you feel faint.
If you feel dizzy while standing, sit down and place your head between your knees or lie on your side until it passes.
When to Call the Office Immediately
Seek prompt evaluation if dizziness occurs with any of the following:
Warning Signs
• Fainting or loss of consciousness
• Chest pain or shortness of breath
• Severe headache
• Vision changes
• Heavy vaginal bleeding
• Severe abdominal or pelvic pain
• Shoulder pain
• Persistent vomiting
• Palpitations or irregular heartbeat
• Sudden swelling of face or hands
These symptoms may require urgent evaluation.
Important Safety Tips
Avoid driving if you are feeling dizzy.
Use handrails when walking on stairs.
Avoid standing for long periods without moving.
Sit down if you feel symptoms coming on.
Reassurance
In most cases, pregnancy-related dizziness is temporary and improves with simple measures. However, it is always appropriate to
mention symptoms at your prenatal visits so we can ensure there is no underlying concern.
If you have questions or your symptoms worsen, please contact our office.

🏃‍♀️Exercise During Pregnancy
ACOG recommends 150 minutes/week of moderate activity — safe for most pregnancies
BENEFITS OF EXERCISE
✓ Reduces gestational diabetes risk by up to 30%
✓ Lowers risk of preeclampsia and hypertension
✓ Reduces back pain and discomfort
✓ Improves mood, sleep, and energy levels
✓ Shorter labor and lower C-section rate
✓ Reduces risk of excessive weight gain
✓ Promotes faster postpartum recovery
ACOG RECOMMENDATIONS
150 min/week of moderate aerobic activity
Spread across most days of the week
"Talk test" — you should be able to speak comfortably
Warm up 5 min before, cool down 5 min after
Stay well hydrated throughout
Avoid exercising in heat or humidity
After 20 weeks, avoid lying flat on back >2–3 min
SAFE ACTIVITIES
SAFE
Walking — excellent starting point for all fitness levels
Swimming and water aerobics — low impact, joint-friendly
Stationary cycling — no fall risk
Prenatal yoga and Pilates — with certified instructor
Low-impact aerobics
Strength training with light-to-moderate weights
Elliptical trainer
ACTIVITIES TO AVOID
AVOID
Contact sports (soccer, basketball, hockey)
Activities with fall risk (skiing, gymnastics, horseback riding)
Scuba diving (fetal decompression sickness risk)
Hot yoga or hot tubs (>102°F / 39°C)
High-altitude exercise (>6,000 feet if not acclimatized)
Exercises requiring lying flat on back after 20 weeks
Heavy weightlifting / Valsalva maneuver
CONTRAINDICATIONS
Exercise should be limited or avoided if you have:
Placenta previa after 26 weeks
Preterm labor or risk of preterm birth
Severe anemia (Hgb <10 g/dL)
Uncontrolled hypertension or heart disease
Incompetent cervix or cerclage in place
Preeclampsia or pregnancy-induced hypertension

🩸 Nosebleeds During Pregnancy
Common in pregnancy and usually not dangerous — here is exactly what to do when one starts
WHY NOSEBLEEDS HAPPEN IN PREGNANCY
•Pregnancy hormones and increased blood flow make the lining inside your nose swollen, dry, and easier to bleed
•Dry air and indoor heating make it worse
•Allergies and colds irritate the nasal lining
•Frequent blowing or irritation inside the nose can also bring one on
•Most pregnancy-related nosebleeds improve after delivery
WHAT TO DO WHEN A NOSEBLEED STARTS
1. Stay calm and sit upright
2. Lean slightly forward — do not lean back or lie down. This keeps blood from running down your throat
3. Pinch the soft part of your nose, just below the bony bridge, firmly between your thumb and index finger
4. Hold steady pressure for 10–15 minutes without checking. Breathe through your mouth
5. Afterward, rest quietly and avoid blowing or picking your nose for several hours If bleeding continues, repeat firm pressure for another 10–15 minutes
DO NOT
•Do not tilt your head back
•Do not lie flat during active bleeding
•Do not place tissues, cotton, or other objects deep inside your nose
•Do not blow your nose immediately after bleeding stops
•Do not start over-the-counter nasal sprays or medications for nosebleeds without checking with us first
PREVENTING NOSEBLEEDS
Keeping the inside of your nose moist is the key to preventing repeat nosebleeds:
✓ Use saline nasal spray or saline gel as directed
✓ Run a cool-mist humidifier, especially while sleeping
✓ Drink adequate fluids
✓ Blow your nose gently; avoid nose picking
✓ Avoid smoke, strong chemical fumes, and other nasal irritants
✓ If you use a prescribed nasal spray, use it exactly as directed and tell us if nosebleeds become frequent
CALL OUR OFFICE IF YOU HAVE
•Nosebleeds that happen often or are becoming more frequent · A nosebleed that does not stop after 20 minutes of correct, firm pressure
•A large amount of bleeding, or bleeding that runs into your mouth or throat · Easy bruising, bleeding gums, unusual vaginal bleeding, or other bleeding concerns
•A history of a bleeding disorder, or use of aspirin, anticoagulants, or other medications that affect bleeding
⚠ CALL 911 OR GO TO THE EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT IF A NOSEBLEED COMES WITH
⚠ Fainting, severe dizziness, or weakness
⚠ Shortness of breath, chest pain, or a rapid heartbeat
⚠ Heavy bleeding that will not stop with firm pressure
⚠ Significant injury to the nose, face, or head
⚠ Severe headache, vision changes, or right upper abdominal pain
⚠ Sudden swelling of the face or hands
💚 Firm Pressure, 10–15 Minutes, Without Peeking

Nosebleeds can be alarming, especially in pregnancy, but they are common and most stop with correct, patient pressure — the most frequent mistake is letting go too early to check. Most pregnancy-related nosebleeds improve after delivery. Please let us know if you have questions or need help managing recurring symptoms.

blocks.text: Round Ligament Pain
Understanding a Common Pregnancy Discomfort
What Is Round Ligament Pain?
Round ligament pain is a common and normal part of
pregnancy. Thick ligaments (called round ligaments)
hold your uterus in place. As your uterus grows, these
ligaments stretch and thin out. The pulling and tugging
can irritate nearby nerves, causing sharp or aching pain
— most often on the right side of the lower abdomen or
pelvis.
Common Symptoms
• Sharp, sudden pain or spasm on one or both sides of
the lower abdomen
• Pain triggered by quick movements — rolling over in
bed, standing up, coughing, or sneezing
• A dull ache after a busy or active day
• Pain that is brief and resolves on its own
When Does It Happen?
Round ligament pain is most common during the
second trimester (around 14–27 weeks) as the uterus
is growing rapidly, but it can occur at any point during
pregnancy. It typically resolves completely after delivery.
Tips for Relief
• Change positions slowly — avoid sudden twisting
or turning
• Rest — lie on the opposite side of the pain with a
pillow between your knees
• Warm compress — apply a heating pad on low or
take a warm bath
• Prenatal stretching — gentle yoga or pelvic tilts can
reduce tension
• Supportive belt — a maternity support band may
ease ligament strain
• Acetaminophen (Tylenol) — safe to take as directed
for persistent pain
When to Call Your Provider
Contact your provider or go to the ER if your pain is
accompanied by:
• Fever, chills, or nausea / vomiting
• Pain or burning with urination
• Vaginal bleeding or unusual discharge
• Pain that is severe, constant, or worsening
• Contractions (tightening at regular intervals)
• Difficulty walking
These symptoms may indicate a urinary tract infection, preterm labor, or another condition that requires evaluation.
The good news: round ligament pain resolves completely after delivery!
This handout is for educational purposes only and does not replace medical advice. Always consult your provider with concerns.

✈️Travel During Pregnancy
Safe travel planning for expectant mothers — air, car, and international tips
BEST TIME TO TRAVEL

The second trimester (14–28 weeks) is generally the safest and most comfortable time to travel. Morning sickness has usually resolved, energy is better, and the risk of miscarriage and preterm labor is lowest. Avoid non-essential travel after 36 weeks — labor can occur unpredictably.
WHO SHOULD AVOID TRAVEL
Preterm labor risk or history of preterm birth
Placenta previa or placental abruption
Uncontrolled hypertension or preeclampsia
Incompetent cervix or cerclage
Multiple pregnancy (especially after 28 weeks)
Severe anemia
Always get medical clearance before long trips
AIR TRAVEL
✓ Generally safe through 36 weeks for uncomplicated pregnancies
Most airlines restrict travel after 36 weeks (some after 28 weeks for international)
Get an aisle seat for easy bathroom access
Walk every 1–2 hours to prevent blood clots
Wear compression stockings (15–30 mmHg)
Stay hydrated — aircraft air is very dry
Radiation from cosmic rays at altitude is minimal for occasional flights
✈ Bring a physician letter stating your due date for flights after 28 weeks — most airlines require it.
CAR TRAVEL
Wear seatbelt correctly: lap belt BELOW the belly, shoulder belt between breasts and to the side of belly
Stop every 1.5–2 hours to walk and stretch
Avoid long trips in third trimester if possible
Keep water and healthy snacks available
Do not travel alone on very long trips
Move seat back as far as comfortable from airbag
INTERNATIONAL TRAVEL CONSIDERATIONS
Research medical care availability at your destination
Check CDC travel health advisories before booking
✗ AVOID areas with Zika virus transmission
✗ AVOID areas with malaria (especially sub-Saharan Africa)
Travel insurance with repatriation coverage essential
Bring prenatal records and blood type card
Know your Rh status and blood type
VACCINES & MEDICATIONS FOR TRAVEL
✓ Safe: Tdap, influenza (inactivated), hepatitis A/B, rabies
✗ Avoid: Live vaccines (typhoid oral, yellow fever, MMR, varicella)
Malaria prophylaxis: Chloroquine/Atovaquone-proguanil generally safe RX
✗ Doxycycline for malaria — AVOID in pregnancy
DEET insect repellent — safe when used as directed OTC
Consult travel medicine clinic 4–6 weeks before departure
⚠ SEEK MEDICAL ATTENTION WHILE TRAVELING IF
Vaginal bleeding or fluid leaking
Severe abdominal pain
Signs of DVT: calf pain, redness, leg swelling
Decreased fetal movement
Regular uterine contractions or cramping
Severe headache, vision changes
High fever or illness
Sudden shortness of breath (PE)

💚 With Good Planning, Travel Can Be Safe and Enjoyable Many pregnant women travel safely throughout their pregnancies. The key is choosing the right time, the right destination, and taking sensible precautions. Talk to your doctor before booking a significant trip — especially international travel — and enjoy your "babymoon" with confidence. Memories made now are precious!

🧬 Tay-Sachs Disease Carrier Screening
Understanding carrier screening and your pregnancy options. Screening is optional — its purpose is to give you information for your decisions.
WHAT IS TAY-SACHS DISEASE?
•A rare inherited disorder that affects the brain and nervous system
•Caused by changes in a gene called HEXA
•The body can't make enough of an enzyme that breaks down fatty substances in nerve cells
•The most common form begins in infancy; rarer forms start in childhood or adulthood
WHAT DOES BEING A CARRIER MEAN?
•A carrier has one working and one changed copy of the HEXA gene
•Carriers are healthy and do not develop Tay-Sachs disease
•The condition is passed down in an autosomal recessive pattern
•A child must inherit a changed gene from both parents to be affected
THE ODDS IF BOTH PARENTS CARRY IT
•25% (1 in 4) chance the child will have Tay-Sachs disease
•50% (1 in 2) chance the child will be a healthy carrier
•25% (1 in 4) chance the child will neither have it nor carry it
•These odds are the same with every pregnancy
WHO SHOULD CONSIDER SCREENING?
✓ Anyone planning or already in a pregnancy may consider it
✓ Especially Ashkenazi Jewish, French Canadian, Cajun, or Pennsylvania Dutch ancestry
✓ A family history of Tay-Sachs or a known HEXA change
✓ Carriers occur in all backgrounds — testing may be offered to anyone
HOW SCREENING IS DONE
•Genetic testing looks for changes in the HEXA gene
•Enzyme testing measures hexosaminidase A activity
•The right test depends on ancestry, family history, and pregnancy status
•If pregnant or on birth control pills, a blood-cell (leukocyte) enzyme test is preferred
•A negative result greatly lowers — but never fully removes — carrier risk
IF YOUR SCREEN IS POSITIVE
•A positive result does not mean you have Tay-Sachs disease
•If one partner is a carrier, the other partner should be tested
•If both are carriers, genetic counseling explains your options

🦠Group B Streptococcus (GBS)
Testing, prevention, and protecting your newborn during labor and delivery
WHAT IS GBS?

Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is a type of bacteria naturally found in the digestive and genital tract. About 10–30% of pregnant women carry GBS. It causes no illness in the mother but can be passed to the baby during birth and cause serious infection. It is NOT a sexually transmitted infection.
HOW & WHEN YOU'RE TESTED
Routine vaginal-rectal swab at 35–37 weeks
Results in 1–5 days
Carrier status can change — test each pregnancy
If GBS positive in urine during pregnancy — treat & assume positive for delivery
If GBS status unknown at delivery — treat based on risk factors
TREATMENT DURING LABOR
IV Penicillin G — first-line antibiotic RX
Given every 4 hours during labor until delivery
Ampicillin — alternative RX
Cefazolin — for penicillin allergy (low-risk) RX
Clindamycin / Vancomycin — severe penicillin allergy RX
Antibiotics must be given at least 4 hours before delivery to be most effective
WHO NEEDS ANTIBIOTICS IN LABOR
GBS-positive culture result at 35–37 weeks
GBS bacteriuria (in urine) during this pregnancy
Previous baby with GBS disease
GBS status unknown AND any of the following:
— Delivery <37 weeks gestation
— Water broken ≥18 hours before delivery
— Fever during labor ≥100.4°F
GBS IN NEWBORNS
Early-onset: 0–6 days of life; pneumonia, meningitis, sepsis
Late-onset: 7 days–3 months; bloodstream or meningitis
Risk to baby reduced by 80%+ with intrapartum antibiotics
Babies observed closely for 24–48 hours after birth
Most GBS-exposed babies remain healthy
Without treatment: ~1–2% of GBS+ mothers have infected babies. With treatment: risk drops to ~0.1%.
GBS IN PREGNANCY (RARE)
GBS can occasionally cause UTI during pregnancy
Treated with oral antibiotics (amoxicillin, nitrofurantoin) RX
Rarely causes chorioamnionitis (uterine infection)
Not necessary to treat vaginal carrier state before labor
Preterm labor may prompt early treatment decisions
⚠ WATCH YOUR NEWBORN FOR THESE SIGNS OF GBS INFECTION
Fever or low temperature in newborn
Grunting, fast breathing, or difficulty breathing
Limpness or stiffness
Bulging fontanelle (soft spot on head)
Poor feeding or extreme sleepiness
Pale, bluish, or blotchy skin color
Irritability or high-pitched cry
Seizures — go to ER immediately

💚 A Positive GBS Test Is Common — Not Dangerous with Proper Care Testing positive for GBS is not a reflection of hygiene or sexual history. It is simply part of your body's normal bacterial environment. With IV antibiotics given during labor, the risk to your baby is dramatically reduced and most GBS-positive mothers have perfectly healthy newborns.

🩸Rh Negative Blood Type in Pregnancy
Understanding Rh sensitization and how RhoGAM protects your baby
WHAT IS RH FACTOR?

The Rh factor is a protein on the surface of red blood cells. If you have it, you are Rh-positive (+). If not, you are Rh-negative (−). About 15% of people are Rh-negative. If you are Rh− and your baby is Rh+ (from the father), your immune system may see the baby's blood cells as "foreign" and make antibodies against them.
WHY DOES IT MATTER?
In a first pregnancy, sensitization rarely causes problems
In subsequent Rh+ pregnancies, antibodies cross the placenta and attack baby's red blood cells
This causes hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN) — anemia, jaundice, heart failure
Risk increases with each untreated sensitizing event
Prevention with RhoGAM is highly effective
RHOGAM INJECTION SCHEDULE
28 weeks — routine prenatal RhoGAM injection if unsensitized After delivery — within 72 hours, if baby is Rh+
After miscarriage — regardless of gestational age After amniocentesis or CVS
After trauma/bleeding — any event that may mix blood
After external cephalic version (ECV)
WHAT IS RHOGAM?
RhoGAM is Rh immune globulin (anti-D) RX
Given as an IM injection (arm or buttock)
Works by "mopping up" any Rh+ fetal cells in your bloodstream before your immune system can respond
Does NOT protect you if you are already sensitized
Safe during pregnancy — does not harm the baby
Protection lasts approximately 12 weeks
SENSITIZING EVENTS REQUIRING RHOGAM
Vaginal bleeding during pregnancy
Miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, or termination
Amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling (CVS)
Abdominal trauma (fall, car accident)
External cephalic version (baby turning)
Manual placenta removal
Placental abruption
IF ALREADY SENSITIZED
Titer testing to measure antibody levels
Serial Doppler ultrasounds of baby's brain blood flow (MCA-PSV)
If fetal anemia detected, intrauterine blood transfusion possible
Close monitoring by maternal-fetal medicine specialist
Neonatology team present at delivery
RhoGAM will NOT help once sensitized
⚠ CALL YOUR DOCTOR IF YOU ARE RH− AND EXPERIENCE
Any vaginal bleeding at any point in pregnancy
Signs of miscarriage (cramping + bleeding)
More than 72 hours have passed since delivery of Rh+ baby
New pregnancy — inform your doctor of Rh status early
Abdominal trauma or a car accident
You missed your 28-week RhoGAM injection
Decreased fetal movement after sensitizing event
Any invasive prenatal procedure not yet followed by RhoGAM

💚 RhoGAM Has Virtually Eliminated Rh Disease Before RhoGAM was introduced in 1968, Rh incompatibility was a leading cause of newborn death and disability. Today, with timely injections, the risk of sensitization is less than 1%. This is one of modern medicine's great success stories — and your diligence in receiving your RhoGAM shots is all that is needed to protect your baby.

🫁RSV in Pregnancy
Protecting you and your newborn from Respiratory Syncytial Virus — the #1 cause of infant hospitalization
400 W Medical Center Blvd, Suite 300 Webster, Texas 77598 · (281) 557-0300
🦠 WHAT IS RSV?

Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) is a common respiratory virus that causes cold-like symptoms in most adults but can be extremely dangerous for newborns and infants, especially in the first 6 months of life.
⚠️ RSV in Infants Can Cause:

Bronchiolitis (lower airway inflammation) Pneumonia Difficulty breathing — hospitalization required RSV is the #1 cause of infant hospitalization in the US ~58,000–80,000 children <5 years hospitalized annually
ℹ️ RSV Season:
Peak season: October through March Spreads via respiratory droplets and surfaces Adults can spread RSV even with mild or no symptoms
💉 RSV VACCINE IN PREGNANCY
Abrysvo® RSV Vaccine

Pfizer — FDA approved for use in pregnancy ⏰ Timing: 32–36 weeks of pregnancy (September–January) A single-dose injection given to the pregnant person. Antibodies cross the placenta, providing passive immunity to the newborn from birth through the most vulnerable first months of life.
✅ Vaccine Benefits:

Reduces severe RSV in infants by ~69% in first 6 months Reduces infant hospitalization for RSV Protection begins immediately at birth — no waiting Safe for both mother and baby based on clinical trials
🍼 NIRSEVIMAB (BEYFORTUS®)
If the RSV vaccine was not received during pregnancy, your newborn can receive Nirsevimab (Beyfortus®) — a monoclonal antibody injection — shortly after birth.
✅ Nirsevimab Facts:

Not a vaccine — it's a preventive antibody injection Recommended for all infants born during or entering RSV season Single dose given at birth or first RSV season Reduces severe RSV illness by ~76% in clinical trials Given at the hospital after delivery or by your pediatrician
Note: Both vaccine and nirsevimab may be used, but the vaccine provides similar
protection — discuss timing with Dr. Klein.
🛡️ ADDITIONAL PROTECTION TIPS
🤲Hand hygiene: Wash hands frequently — ask everyone to wash before
holding newborn
😷Sick visitors: No visiting if anyone has cold/respiratory symptoms
🏠Avoid crowds: Limit exposure of newborns to public places during RSV
season (Oct–March)
🚭No smoking: Secondhand smoke significantly increases RSV severity in
infants
🤱Breastfeeding: Provides antibodies and additional immune protection to
your baby 🚨 If Your Baby Shows These Signs, Seek Care Immediately:
Rapid or labored breathing, flared nostrils Blue lips or fingernails (cyanosis) Not eating well, extreme fatigue
The RSV Vaccine Is One of the Most Impactful Things You Can Do for Your Newborn

We strongly recommend the RSV vaccine for all eligible pregnant patients between 32–36 weeks. This simple step can keep your baby out of the hospital during their most vulnerable first months. Questions? Call us at

6a0ba963.title: Vacunas durante el embarazo
6a0ba963.subtitle: Información sobre las vacunas durante el embarazo.
6a0ba963.author: Geffrey H. Klein, MD
6a0ba963.address: 400 W Medical Center Blvd, Suite 300, Webster, TX 77598

blocks.text: Probablemente ya sabes que cuando estás embarazada, compartes todo con tu bebé. Eso significa que cuando te vacunas, no solo te proteges a ti misma, sino que también le das a tu bebé una protección temprana.
Vacuna contra la Tos Ferina (TDAP)

La tos ferina (o pertussis) puede ser grave para cualquiera, pero para tu recién nacido, puede ser mortal. Hasta 20 bebés mueren cada año en Estados Unidos debido a la tos ferina. Alrededor de la mitad de los bebés menores de 1 año que contraen tos ferina necesitan tratamiento en el hospital. Cuanto más joven sea el bebé cuando contraiga la tos ferina, más probable es que necesite ser tratado en un hospital. Puede ser difícil para ti saber si tu bebé tiene tos ferina porque muchos bebés con esta enfermedad no tosen en absoluto. En cambio, puede hacer que dejen de respirar y se pongan azules. Cuando te vacunas contra la tos ferina durante tu embarazo, tu cuerpo creará anticuerpos protectores y pasará algunos de ellos a tu bebé antes del nacimiento. Estos anticuerpos proporcionarán a tu bebé una protección temprana y a corto plazo contra la tos ferina. La TDAP se administra al entrar en el tercer trimestre.
Aprende más en www.cdc.gov/pertussis/pregnant/.
Vacuna contra la Gripe

Los cambios en tus funciones inmunológicas, cardíacas y pulmonares durante el embarazo te hacen más propensa a enfermarte gravemente de la gripe. Contraer la gripe también aumenta tus posibilidades de problemas graves para tu bebé en desarrollo, incluyendo parto prematuro y nacimiento. Vacúnate contra la gripe si estás embarazada durante la temporada de gripe, es la mejor manera de protegerte a ti y a tu bebé durante varios meses después del nacimiento de complicaciones relacionadas con la gripe.

Las temporadas de gripe varían en su momento de una temporada a otra, pero los CDC recomiendan vacunarse a finales de octubre, si es posible. Este momento ayuda a protegerte antes de que la actividad de la gripe comience a aumentar.
Encuentra más sobre cómo prevenir la gripe visitando www.cdc.gov/flu/.
¿Debo vacunarme contra el VRS durante el embarazo?

ACOG recomienda la vacuna Pfizer RSV si estás de 32 a 36 semanas de embarazo de septiembre a enero. La vacuna crea anticuerpos que pasan a tu feto. Esto significa que el bebé tendrá algunos anticuerpos para protegerse del VRS durante los primeros 6 meses después del nacimiento.

El VRS, o virus sincitial respiratorio, es un virus que se propaga en otoño e invierno. El VRS puede ser peligroso para bebés y niños pequeños. Es la principal causa de hospitalización entre los bebés en Estados Unidos.

Hay varias vacunas contra el VRS aprobadas por la Administración de Alimentos y Medicamentos de EE. UU. (FDA). La única vacuna contra el VRS aprobada por la FDA para su uso en el embarazo es la fabricada por Pfizer, llamada Abrysvo.

Puedes recibir la vacuna Pfizer RSV al mismo tiempo que otras vacunas recomendadas durante el embarazo. Los efectos secundarios comunes de la vacuna contra el VRS incluyen dolor en el brazo, dolor de cabeza, dolor muscular y náuseas, similares a otros efectos secundarios de las vacunas. Los efectos secundarios son normales y no son motivo de preocupación.
Encuentra más en https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines/vpd/rsv/public/pregnancy.html.

🫀Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy (ICP)
A liver condition causing intense itching — requires monitoring and management
WHAT IS ICP?

Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP) is a liver condition where bile acids build up in the blood because bile flow from the liver slows. It typically appears in the second or third trimester. It affects about 1–2 in 1,000 pregnancies in the U.S., and is more common in women of South American or Scandinavian descent.
RISK FACTORS
Personal or family history of ICP
Previous ICP pregnancy (recurrence risk 60–70%)
Twin or multiple pregnancy
Gallbladder disease or gallstones
South American, Scandinavian, or Chilean heritage
Hepatitis C infection
Prior oral contraceptive pill-induced liver issues
SYMPTOMS
Intense itching — especially palms and soles, worse at night
No rash (distinguishes ICP from PUPPS)
Dark urine or pale/greasy stools
Mild jaundice (yellowing of skin/eyes) — rare
Fatigue and loss of appetite
Right upper abdominal discomfort
Itching often worsens as pregnancy progresses
DIAGNOSIS
Serum bile acids — key diagnostic test
Liver function tests (ALT, AST, bilirubin)
Values typically elevated by 3rd trimester
Bile acids ≥10 µmol/L diagnostic; ≥40 µmol/L severe
Ultrasound to evaluate gallbladder
Repeat labs every 1–2 weeks to monitor
TREATMENT
Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) — first-line treatment RX
UDCA reduces bile acids, improves itching
Antihistamines (Benadryl) for itch relief OTC
Sarna lotion, cool baths, loose cotton clothing
Weekly nonstress tests starting at 32–34 weeks
Early delivery typically recommended at 37 weeks
Vitamin K supplement may be prescribed
FETAL RISKS
Increased risk of preterm birth
Fetal distress during labor
Stillbirth risk — especially with bile acids ≥40 µmol/L
Meconium-stained fluid
Risk correlates with severity of bile acid elevation
Condition resolves for mother after delivery
⚠ CALL YOUR DOCTOR RIGHT AWAY
New onset of intense itching, especially at night
Jaundice (yellow skin or eyes)
Fever with abdominal pain
Itching spreading to rest of body
Decreased fetal movement
Dark urine or pale stools
Contractions before 37 weeks
Right upper quadrant pain

💚 With Careful Monitoring, Outcomes Are Excellent ICP is treatable and manageable with close monitoring. Most babies born to mothers with ICP do very well, especially when the condition is caught early and managed with medication and timely delivery. Itching typically resolves within days of delivery. Your team will keep you and your baby safe every step of the way.

🩸Gestational Diabetes (GDM)
Managing blood sugar during pregnancy to protect you and your baby
WHAT IS GDM?

Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar that develops during pregnancy in women who didn't have diabetes before. It occurs in 6–9% of pregnancies. The placenta produces hormones that can block insulin's action (insulin resistance). When the pancreas can't keep up, blood glucose rises.
RISK FACTORS
BMI ≥25 (overweight or obesity)
Family history of type 2 diabetes
Previous GDM or large baby (>9 lbs)
Hispanic, Black, Asian, or Native American heritage
Age over 35
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
Prediabetes before pregnancy
BLOOD GLUCOSE GOALS
Check blood sugar 4 times daily: fasting + after each meal. Log results and bring to every visit.
DIET MANAGEMENT
Distribute carbs throughout 3 meals + 2–3 snacks
Breakfast carbs limited (15–30g) — morning insulin resistance highest
Choose complex carbs: whole grains, legumes, vegetables
Avoid sugary drinks, juice, white bread, white rice
Pair carbs with protein and healthy fat at every meal
Work with a registered dietitian for meal planning
MEDICAL MANAGEMENT
Diet + exercise controls GDM in ~70–80% of cases
Insulin — first-line medication when needed RX
Metformin — oral option, crosses placenta RX
Weekly monitoring appointments once on medication
Nonstress tests starting at 32–36 weeks
Ultrasound to check fetal growth (possible macrosomia)
Delivery planning based on glucose control
RISKS IF UNCONTROLLED
Baby: Macrosomia (large baby), birth injury, low blood sugar at birth, jaundice, preterm birth, increased future diabetes risk
Mother: C-section, preeclampsia, type 2 diabetes risk (50% within 10 years)
GDM usually resolves after delivery
Postpartum glucose test at 6–12 weeks required
⚠ CALL YOUR DOCTOR IF YOU EXPERIENCE
Fasting blood sugar consistently over 100 mg/dL
Severe headache or blurred vision
Decreased fetal movement
Nausea/vomiting preventing you from eating
After-meal readings over 140–150 mg/dL
Excessive thirst or urination
Signs of low blood sugar: shakiness, sweating, confusion
Illness or infection (can spike blood sugar)

💚 Gestational Diabetes Is Very Manageable Most women with GDM have healthy pregnancies and healthy babies with the right care. You have significant control over your blood sugar through what you eat and how you move. Every healthy meal and every walk around the block is a gift to your baby. You are doing an amazing job — keep going!

Severe headache unrelieved by Tylenol Sudden severe upper abdominal pain Seizure or loss of consciousness Sudden swelling of face or hands

💚 With Close Monitoring, Most Women Have Healthy Outcomes Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are among the most monitored and managed conditions in obstetrics. When caught early and treated appropriately, most women — and their babies — do very well. Placenta Previa
A low-lying placenta can be managed safely with careful monitoring and a planned delivery
WHAT IS PLACENTA PREVIA?
A condition where the placenta lies low in the uterus and covers all or part of the cervix
The placenta provides oxygen and nutrients to your baby
When it blocks the cervix, it can cause bleeding and make vaginal delivery unsafe
Occurs in about 1 in 200 pregnancies at delivery
Many low placentas found early in pregnancy move upward as the uterus grows
RISK FACTORS
Prior cesarean delivery or uterine surgery
Previous placenta previa
Multiple prior pregnancies
Smoking during pregnancy
Twin or multiple pregnancy
Advanced maternal age
Use of IVF or assisted reproduction
HOW IT IS DIAGNOSED
Diagnosed by ultrasound, often during your routine anatomy scan
Transvaginal ultrasound is safe and most accurate
Follow-up ultrasound usually done at 32 weeks, sometimes again at 36 weeks
Most common symptom: painless vaginal bleeding in the 2nd or 3rd trimester
Some women have no symptoms at all
MANAGEMENT & DELIVERY
If not bleeding: avoid intercourse, nothing in the vagina, no heavy lifting
If bleeding: hospital admission, IV fluids, fetal monitoring
Planned cesarean delivery at 36-37 weeks if placenta still covers cervix
Earlier delivery if bleeding is heavy or persistent
Vaginal delivery may be possible if placenta is low but not covering cervix
Delivery planned at hospital with blood bank services
POSSIBLE COMPLICATIONS
Heavy bleeding before or during delivery
Preterm birth
Need for blood transfusion
Cesarean delivery
Increased risk of placenta accreta (placenta attaches too deeply), especially with prior C-sections
Rarely, hysterectomy may be needed
WHAT YOU CAN DO
Keep all prenatal appointments and follow-up ultrasounds
No sexual intercourse and nothing inserted in the vagina
Avoid strenuous activity and heavy lifting
Stay close to a hospital and know your route
Do not allow a digital cervical exam until previa is ruled out
Discuss a delivery plan with your provider in advance
⚠GO TO THE HOSPITAL IMMEDIATELY IF YOU EXPERIENCE
Any vaginal bleeding, even light spotting
Regular contractions
Abdominal or pelvic pain
Decreased baby movements
Leaking fluid from the vagina
Signs of labor
Lightheadedness or fainting
Rapid heartbeat or weakness
You Are Not Alone -- We Are Here to Guide You

Most women with placenta previa have healthy babies and deliver safely with planned cesarean. Many cases diagnosed early resolve on their own as pregnancy progresses. With close monitoring and a clear delivery plan, outcomes are excellent. Please call us any time you have questions or concerns -- we are here for you every step of the way.

PUPPS Rash in Pregnancy
Pruritic Urticarial Papules and Plaques of Pregnancy — intensely itchy but benign
WHAT IS PUPPS?

PUPPS (Pruritic Urticarial Papules and Plaques of Pregnancy) is the most common pregnancy-specific rash, affecting 1 in 160–200 pregnancies. It causes intensely itchy red bumps and hive-like plaques, usually starting in the stretch marks on the abdomen. It is benign — poses no risk to the baby.
WHO GETS PUPPS?
Most common in first pregnancies (primigravidas)
Usually appears in the 3rd trimester (35–39 weeks)
More common with large weight gain or large babies
Much more common in twin pregnancies
More common when carrying a male fetus
Rare in subsequent pregnancies (usually doesn't recur)
HOW PUPPS LOOKS & SPREADS
Starts in abdominal stretch marks (striae)
Spreads to thighs, buttocks, and arms
Small red or skin-colored bumps (papules)
Hive-like plaques that may merge
Intense itching — often worst at night
Spares the face, hands, and feet
No blistering (distinguishes from pemphigoid)
Umbilicus usually spared (unlike cholestasis)
PUPPS VS. ICP (CHOLESTASIS)
SOOTHING TREATMENTS
✓ Cool oatmeal baths (Aveeno) OTC
✓ Sarna lotion (menthol/camphor) — cooling relief OTC
✓ Calamine lotion OTC
✓ Benadryl (diphenhydramine) at bedtime OTC
✓ Hydrocortisone 1% cream — mild topical steroid OTC
✓ Cold compresses on affected areas
✓ Loose, cotton, breathable clothing
✗ Avoid hot showers/baths — worsens itching
MEDICAL TREATMENTS
Prescription topical steroids — triamcinolone, betamethasone cream RX
Oral antihistamines — hydroxyzine RX
Short course of oral prednisone — for severe PUPPS RX
PUPPS resolves within 1–4 weeks of delivery
Delivery is ultimately the cure
Dermatology referral if diagnosis uncertain
⚠ CALL YOUR DOCTOR IF
New rash or itching that starts in the 3rd trimester
Itching on palms/soles without a visible rash (rule out ICP)
Itching so severe you cannot sleep for multiple nights
No improvement with OTC treatments after 48–72 hours
Blisters or vesicles appear (may indicate pemphigoid)
Rash spreads to face or becomes infected
Fever accompanying the rash
Dark urine or jaundice — could indicate cholestasis

💚 PUPPS Is Miserable, But Harmless to Your Baby We know PUPPS itching can be truly overwhelming — it is one of the most uncomfortable pregnancy conditions. The good news: your baby is completely unaffected. With the right treatments to manage the itch, most women get through it. Delivery brings complete resolution, usually within a week or two.

Thyroid Disorders in Pregnancy
Thyroid hormone is essential for your baby's brain development -- with proper monitoring, most women have healthy pregnancies
WHY THE THYROID MATTERS
The thyroid makes hormones that control metabolism,
energy, and temperature
Your body needs more thyroid hormone during pregnancy
Your baby depends on your thyroid for brain development, especially in the first trimester
Thyroid disorders affect about 2-3% of pregnancies
Most cases are safely managed with medication and monitoring
HYPOTHYROIDISM (UNDERACTIVE)
Symptoms: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin
Risks if untreated: miscarriage, preeclampsia, preterm birth, low birth weight
Treated with levothyroxine -- safe in pregnancy
Most women on thyroid medication need a dose increase during pregnancy
Blood tests checked every 4-6 weeks
HYPERTHYROIDISM (OVERACTIVE)
Most often caused by Graves' disease
Symptoms: rapid heartbeat, weight loss, anxiety, tremors, heat intolerance
Risks if untreated: miscarriage, preterm delivery, low birth weight, fetal thyroid problems
Treated with antithyroid medication at the lowest effective dose
Requires frequent blood testing
WHO NEEDS THYROID TESTING?
Personal or family history of thyroid disease
Autoimmune disorders (such as Type 1 diabetes)
Prior thyroid surgery or radiation
Symptoms of thyroid dysfunction
Women on thyroid medication should be tested early in pregnancy
IODINE, BREASTFEEDING & POSTPARTUM
Aim for 200-250 mcg iodine daily from prenatal vitamins and diet
Do not take extra iodine unless instructed
Levothyroxine is safe while breastfeeding
Most antithyroid medications are safe at appropriate doses
Postpartum thyroiditis can occur within the first year after delivery -- follow-up labs may be needed
PLANNING PREGNANCY
Make sure thyroid levels are stable before conceiving
Contact your physician as soon as pregnancy is confirmed
Early medication adjustments are often needed
Continue prenatal vitamins with iodine
Keep all scheduled lab appointments
⚠CALL YOUR DOCTOR IF YOU EXPERIENCE
Palpitations or rapid heartbeat
Severe fatigue or weakness
Sudden weight loss or weight gain
Swelling in the neck, hands, or face
Severe headaches or elevated blood pressure
Heat or cold intolerance that is new
Anxiety, tremors, or mood changes
Symptoms that worsen during or after pregnancy
Healthy Thyroid, Healthy Pregnancy

Thyroid disease during pregnancy sounds scary, but with regular monitoring and the right medication dose, nearly all women go on to have healthy babies. The key is early testing, consistent follow-up labs, and taking your medication exactly as prescribed. Please bring any questions about your thyroid care to your next visit -- we are here to help.
