Big Baby? Should I Be Induced at 38 Weeks?
New high-quality evidence (Lancet 2025, AJOG-MFM 2026) supports offering induction at 38+0 to 38+4 weeks when baby's estimated weight is >90th percentile
WHAT 'LARGE FOR GESTATIONAL AGE' MEANS
LGA = estimated fetal weight (EFW) above the 90th percentile for gestational age, measured by ultrasound
Macrosomia = birth weight ≥ 4,000 g (about 8 lb 13 oz), or ≥ 4,500 g (9 lb 15 oz) for severe macrosomia
Ultrasound estimates of weight are ± 10-15% accurate -- they are a guide, not a guarantee
Most LGA babies are healthy and deliver without complications
Some risks rise with larger babies: shoulder dystocia, fracture during birth, C-section, perineal injury, and (for baby) low blood sugar or jaundice
Risk is higher if you have diabetes -- those patients are managed separately
WHAT THE NEW RESEARCH SHOWS
Big Baby Trial (UK, Lancet 2025) -- 2,893 women with suspected LGA, induced at 38+0 to 38+4 vs. standard care
Shoulder dystocia -- 2.3% (induction) vs. 3.1% (standard); in the per-protocol analysis, induction cut the risk almost in half (2.3% vs 3.7%)
Meta-analysis (AJOG-MFM 2026, 5 trials, ~4,000 women) -- induction at 38 wks reduced cesarean delivery (27.9% vs
Induction also dramatically reduced very large birth weights (≥ 4,000 g cut nearly in half; ≥ 4,500 g cut by ~80%)
Number needed to treat: about 25 inductions to prevent 1
cesarean
Trend toward fewer birth fractures and fewer shoulder dystocia events, though not always statistically significant
WHO THIS APPLIES TO
Single baby, head down, at term
Estimated fetal weight > 90th percentile on an ultrasound between 35-38 weeks
Healthy pregnancy with no other reason for early delivery
No major contraindications to vaginal birth or induction
Not included in the research: patients with gestational or pre-existing diabetes -- those are managed by separate guidelines
Patients already planned for cesarean or with another induction indication
POTENTIAL BENEFITS OF INDUCING AT 38 WEEKS
Lower chance of cesarean delivery (about 4 fewer C- sections per 100 women)
Much lower chance of a very large baby (>4,000 or >4,500 g)
Likely lower risk of shoulder dystocia and the injuries that can come with it
Less time waiting and worrying about size and timing
Babies born at 38 weeks are mature and do well in nearly all cases
More predictable scheduling for you and the delivery team
POTENTIAL DOWNSIDES
More newborn jaundice requiring phototherapy (treatable light therapy) -- the main difference seen in the meta-analysis
Induction takes time -- can be a longer hospital stay before delivery
Some women find induced labor more uncomfortable;
epidural is available
Ultrasound weight estimates can be off -- baby may be smaller than predicted
Induction does not guarantee a vaginal birth; cesarean is still
possible
Earlier birth means slightly less time for some final development (rarely an issue at 38+ weeks)
MAKING THE DECISION TOGETHER
This is a shared decision -- there is no one-size-fits-all answer
We will review your specific ultrasound numbers, history,
and goals
Best evidence supports the 38+0 to 38+4 week window if you choose induction
Standard care (wait for spontaneous labor) is also reasonable, especially if EFW is closer to the 90th percentile
Tell us if you have a strong preference for vaginal birth, an earlier or later delivery, or avoiding induction
Ask about cervical ripeness (Bishop score) -- a favorable cervix makes induction more likely to succeed
Bring your birth partner and questions to the next visit so we can plan together
⚠CALL OR GO TO LABOR & DELIVERY IF YOU EXPERIENCE
Regular, painful contractions (call us)
Your water breaks
Severe abdominal pain
Severe headache, vision changes, or upper-belly pain
Vaginal bleeding more than spotting
Decreased baby movement
Sudden swelling of hands, face, or one leg
Any concern that something feels wrong -- trust your instincts
Good Evidence, Real Choices

Recent high-quality research (the UK Big Baby trial and a 2026 meta-analysis of about 4,000 women) shows that offering induction between 38+0 and 38+4 weeks for babies estimated above the 90th percentile can lower the chance of cesarean delivery and very large birth weight, with a likely reduction in shoulder dystocia. The main trade-off is slightly more newborn jaundice. Both early induction and waiting for spontaneous labor remain reasonable options -- the right choice depends on your numbers, your history, and what matters most to you. Bring your questions; we'll decide together.

👶Breech Presentation
When baby is in a bottom-down or feet-first position near term
WHAT IS BREECH POSITION?

A breech baby has their buttocks or feet positioned to be born first, rather than head-first (vertex). Most babies turn head-down by 36 weeks. Breech occurs in about 3–4% of full-term pregnancies. Many babies are breech earlier in pregnancy and turn on their own.
TYPES OF BREECH
Frank breech — buttocks first, legs extended up
Most Common
Complete breech — sitting cross-legged, bottom first
Footling breech — one or both feet first
Transverse lie — baby lying sideways
RISK FACTORS
Preterm pregnancy (before 37 weeks)
Multiple gestation (twins/triplets)
Uterine abnormalities or fibroids
Placenta previa
Excess amniotic fluid (polyhydramnios)
Previous breech baby
Fetal abnormalities (rare)
HOW IS IT DIAGNOSED?
Leopold maneuvers — hands-on abdominal exam
Ultrasound — confirms position accurately
Usually detected at 35–36 week prenatal visit
You may feel hard round head (kicks) near ribs
Hiccups felt low in pelvis suggest head-down
EXTERNAL CEPHALIC VERSION (ECV)

ECV is a procedure at 36–37 weeks where your doctor manually turns the baby from outside your belly. Performed in the hospital with monitoring. Success rate: ~50–60%. Medication to relax the uterus is used. Risk of complications is low but ECV is not appropriate for all patients.
DELIVERY OPTIONS
C-section — most common recommendation for persistent breech at term; safest option for most
Vaginal breech delivery — rarely offered; requires specific criteria and experienced provider
If baby turns after ECV or spontaneously — normal vaginal birth possible
Decisions made based on your specific situation
⚠ WHEN TO CALL YOUR DOCTOR / GO TO LABOR & DELIVERY
You feel the umbilical cord in your vagina
Vaginal bleeding at any time
Regular contractions before 37 weeks
Any concern about your baby's movement or position
Decreased fetal movement after 28 weeks
Water breaks before labor starts
Sudden severe abdominal pain
Fluid leaking from vagina

💚 Many Breech Babies Turn on Their Own! The majority of babies who are breech before 36 weeks turn to head-down on their own. Even if your baby remains breech, you have safe, well-studied options. Whether through ECV, a planned cesarean, or a spontaneous turn, your care team will guide you toward the safest outcome for you and your baby.

🏥Cesarean Birth (C-Section)
What to expect before, during, and after your surgical delivery
COMMON REASONS FOR C-SECTION
Failure to progress in labor
Non-reassuring fetal heart rate
Breech or transverse baby position
Placenta previa (placenta over cervix)
Prior uterine surgery or classical C-section
Maternal medical conditions (severe preeclampsia)
Multiple gestation in certain positions
TYPES OF C-SECTION
Planned (elective) — scheduled in advance for known indications
Unplanned — decided during labor for a new indication
Emergency — immediate surgery for fetal or maternal distress
Most use a low transverse (bikini line) incision
Classical vertical incision rarely used today
BEFORE SURGERY
NPO (nothing by mouth) 8 hours before
IV line placed; antacid medication given
Spinal or epidural anesthesia — you stay awake
Foley catheter placed after anesthesia
Abdomen prepped and sterile drape placed
Support person may be present in OR
Surgery typically takes 45–60 minutes total
DURING THE PROCEDURE
You will feel pressure and pulling — not pain
Baby is usually delivered within first 5–10 min
Delayed cord clamping when safe
Skin-to-skin contact in OR when possible
Uterus and layers closed; 4–6 skin sutures or staples
Gentle tummy tuck style closure used
RECOVERY — FIRST 24 HOURS
Recovery room monitoring 1–2 hours post-op
Foley catheter removed within 12–24 hours
Begin walking as soon as anesthesia wears off
Pain managed with scheduled ibuprofen + Tylenol
Narcotic pain meds available if needed RX
Hospital stay typically 3 days
Breastfeeding supported immediately
RECOVERY AT HOME
No lifting over 10 lbs for 6 weeks
No driving for 2 weeks or while on narcotics
Pelvic rest (no sex) for 6 weeks
Keep incision dry; pat clean; no submerging
Activity gradually increases over 6 weeks
Follow-up visit at 2 weeks and 6 weeks post-op
VBAC may be possible for future pregnancies
⚠ CALL YOUR DOCTOR OR GO TO ER AFTER DISCHARGE
Fever over 100.4°F (38°C)
Increasing rather than improving pain
Foul-smelling vaginal discharge
Chest pain or difficulty breathing
Incision red, swollen, draining, or opening
Heavy vaginal bleeding (soaking >1 pad/hour)
Calf pain, redness, or leg swelling (clot?)
Signs of wound dehiscence (incision opening)

💚 A Cesarean Birth Is Still a Beautiful Birth Regardless of how your baby arrives, you are a strong and wonderful mother. A C-section is a major surgery performed to protect you and your baby. Allow yourself to heal — physically and emotionally. Your body has done something remarkable, and your care team is with you every step of the recovery journey.

Dr. Geffrey H. Klein, MD · FACOG · DABOM · 400 W Medical Center Blvd, Suite 300, Webster, TX 77598 · (281) 557-0300
External Cephalic Version (ECV)
A safe procedure to gently turn a breech baby head-down -- giving you a better chance at a vaginal birth
WHAT IS AN ECV?
A procedure where your provider uses firm hands on your belly to gently turn the baby from breech (or sideways) to head-down
Usually performed at 37 weeks of pregnancy -- when baby is mature but still has room to turn
Done in the hospital, with continuous fetal monitoring and an OR available in case an emergency cesarean is needed
Takes only a few minutes, though setup and monitoring make it a half-day visit
Success rate: about 50-60% overall (higher in women who have had a baby before)
Successful ECV greatly lowers your chance of needing a
cesarean
WHO IS A GOOD CANDIDATE?
Single baby in breech, transverse, or oblique position at 36+ weeks
Adequate amniotic fluid and a reactive non-stress test
No placenta previa or other reason a vaginal birth would be unsafe
No prior classical (vertical) cesarean or full-thickness uterine surgery
Intact membranes (water hasn't broken)
Even after a low-transverse cesarean, ECV can be considered with similar success rates
Better odds if you have had a prior vaginal birth, a posterior placenta, plenty of fluid, or a complete (rather than frank) breech
WHEN ECV IS NOT RECOMMENDED
Placenta previa or vasa previa
Prior classical or vertical uterine incision
Active labor with ruptured membranes or significantly engaged breech
Severe oligohydramnios (very low fluid)
Non-reassuring fetal monitoring or signs of distress
Significant fetal anomaly, hyperextended head, or multiple gestation (twins) -- usually
Placental abruption, severe preeclampsia, or HELLP syndrome
Fetal growth restriction -- in most cases
RISKS TO KNOW ABOUT
Overall complication rate is about 6% -- most are minor and resolve quickly
Temporary changes in fetal heart rate (most common; typically resolve within minutes)
Vaginal bleeding or rupture of membranes
Placental abruption -- about 1 in 1,200 attempts
Emergency cesarean delivery -- about 1 in 300 attempts
Stillbirth -- about 1 in 5,000 attempts (very rare)
Small fetomaternal blood transfer -- if you are Rh-negative, you will get Rhogam afterward
Procedure can be uncomfortable but is usually tolerated without anesthesia
HOW TO PREPARE
Drink plenty of water for 24 hours before -- may help by increasing amniotic fluid
Light breakfast is OK; some hospitals ask you not to eat 2-8 hours before in case a cesarean is needed
Wear loose, comfortable clothing -- you'll change into a gown
Bring your partner or support person and your hospital paperwork
Bring your car seat and hospital bag -- if labor begins or a cesarean is needed, you may not go home
Plan to be at the hospital for 3-4 hours total
Avoid driving home alone if you receive medication that may cause sedation
⚠CALL OR GO TO LABOR & DELIVERY IMMEDIATELY FOR
Vaginal bleeding more than light spotting
WHAT TO EXPECT DURING & AFTER
Ultrasound to confirm baby's position, fluid level, and placenta
Fetal heart-rate monitoring before, during, and after
Terbutaline injection (a medication to relax the uterus) is usually given 15-30 min beforehand
Provider applies steady, firm pressure on your belly to roll baby into head-down position
Procedure stops if you have significant pain or baby's heart rate changes
Up to 2-4 attempts may be tried; if unsuccessful, a repeat ECV can be offered another day
Monitoring continues 30-60 minutes after; you go home if all is reassuring
After successful ECV, routine prenatal care resumes -- we wait for spontaneous labor (no immediate induction)
Severe abdominal pain
Leaking fluid (possible rupture of membranes)
Decreased or absent fetal movement
Regular contractions or low back pain
Lightheadedness, fainting, or rapid heartbeat
Fever or chills
Any concern that something is wrong -- trust your instincts
A Reasonable Step Toward a Vaginal Birth

ECV is one of the most evidence-based ways to avoid a cesarean delivery for a breech baby. About half to two-thirds of attempts succeed, and serious complications are rare. Even if it doesn't work, you still have safe options -- a planned cesarean, or in some cases, a vaginal breech delivery. Bring your questions and your birth preferences to your prenatal visit, and we will help you weigh the choice that's right for you and your baby.

Monitoring your baby's movements in the third trimester
Women's Specialists of Clear Lake
Geffrey H. Klein, MD · FACOG · DABOM
WHY KICK COUNTS MATTER

Once you reach the third trimester, counting your baby's movements is one of the easiest and most effective ways to monitor your baby's wellbeing — and it's free and can be done at home. Kick counts help you get to know your baby's normal activity patterns so you can quickly recognize when something feels different. A significant change in movement — more or less than usual — can sometimes be a sign that your baby needs attention. Staying in tune with those movements is one of the best things you can do to keep your baby safe.
HOW TO DO KICK COUNTS

Step 1: Eat a meal or snack — babies are most active after you eat. Step 2: Lie on your side in a comfortable position. Place your hand on your belly. Step 3: Begin counting every movement you feel — kicks, rolls, jabs, and flutters all count. Step 4: Stop when you reach 10 movements. Most babies reach 10 within an hour.

Best times to count:
• After meals — when baby tends to be most active
• In the evening
• After drinking something sweet (juice, milk)

Labor Induction
When and why labor is started with medications or other methods — what to expect during the process
WHAT IS LABOR INDUCTION?
The use of medications or other methods to bring on labor
Goal is to stimulate uterine contractions for a vaginal birth
May be recommended if mother or baby's health is at risk
Elective induction is for nonmedical reasons and should not happen before 39 weeks
Medical reasons include high blood pressure, diabetes, or concerns about the baby
IS YOUR CERVIX READY? (BISHOP SCORE)
Before labor, the cervix naturally softens, thins, and opens
The Bishop score (0–13) rates how ready your cervix is for labor
A score less than 6 means your cervix may not yet be ready
Lower scores mean cervical ripening may be needed first
Higher scores are associated with more successful induction
CERVICAL RIPENING METHODS
Prostaglandins — medications inserted vaginally or taken by mouth to soften the cervix
Some prostaglandins are avoided after prior cesarean due to uterine rupture risk
Foley balloon catheter — a small tube with an inflatable balloon to widen the cervix
Laminaria — a natural substance that absorbs water and gently expands the cervix
Membrane stripping — sweeping a finger along the amniotic sac to release natural prostaglandins
INDUCTION METHODS
Oxytocin (Pitocin) — IV hormone that causes contractions; usually starts within 30 minutes
Amniotomy — breaking the water with a small instrument
Amniotomy is done when the cervix is dilated and thinned and baby's head is low
Most women go into labor within hours of water breaking
Multiple methods may be used together for best results
RISKS OF INDUCTION
Too many contractions (uterine overstimulation) can affect the baby's heart rate
Infection of the mother or baby, especially after water breaks
Uterine rupture — rare but serious, particularly with prior cesarean
Umbilical cord problems
Increased chance of cesarean, especially in first-time mothers with an unripe cervix
WHAT TO EXPECT
Induction can take hours to days — especially if the cervix is not yet ripe
You'll be monitored closely — contractions and baby's heart rate are watched continuously
Pain management options (IV, epidural) are available when you need them
Sometimes induction does not work and cesarean delivery may be needed
Bring comfort items, snacks for your partner, and patience
⚠CALL (281) 557-0300 FOR EMERGENCIES OR IF YOU EXPERIENCE
Heavy vaginal bleeding (more than spotting)
Decreased or no fetal movement
Severe or constant abdominal pain
Severe headache or vision changes
Sudden gush of fluid (water breaking)
Signs of labor: regular, painful contractions
You're Almost There — We're With You Every Step

Labor induction is a safe, common way to help your baby arrive when needed. Our team will explain each step, answer your questions, and support you throughout the process. Don't hesitate to ask anything — we want you to feel informed and confident!

Signs to watch for as your due date approaches

Geffrey H. Klein, MD · FACOG · DABOM

As you approach the end of your pregnancy, your body will begin sending signals that labor may be near. Understanding what to watch for — and knowing when to call or head to Labor & Delivery — will help you feel prepared and confident. Remember: when in doubt, always call us. We would rather hear from you.
I GO TO LABOR & DELIVERY IMMEDIATELY if you experience any of these:
• Heavy vaginal bleeding (more than a normal period)
• Your water breaks (sudden gush or steady trickle of fluid)
• Baby has stopped moving or is moving significantly less
• Severe abdominal pain or pressure
• Contractions before 37 weeks (preterm labor)
• Sudden severe headache, vision changes, or facial swelling

blocks.text: I Pain Relief in Labor
Your options for managing labor pain
Women's Specialists of Clear Lake
Geffrey H. Klein, MD · FACOG · DABOM

Every labor is different — and so is every person's experience of pain. The good news is that you have many options, and you don't have to decide everything in advance. This pamphlet outlines your choices so you can think about what feels right for you and discuss it with your care team.
NON-MEDICATION OPTIONS
These techniques can significantly reduce pain and are safe at any point in labor. Many people use them alongside medication.
Movement & Position
• Walking, rocking, or swaying during contractions
• Hands-and-knees position relieves back labor
• Birthing ball for hip movement and pressure relief
Touch & Heat
• Massage and counterpressure on the lower back
• Warm compress or shower/tub (hydrotherapy)
• Cold pack on the lower back between contractions
Breathing & Relaxation
• Slow, focused breathing through each contraction
• Visualization — imagining a calm, safe place
• Guided relaxation or meditation apps
Support
• Continuous support from a partner, doula, or nurse
significantly reduces pain perception
• Calm environment — dim lights, familiar music, or
quiet
YOUR BIRTH PLAN & PAIN PREFERENCES
MEDICATION OPTIONS

I Epidural Anesthesia The most commonly used and most effective form of pain relief in labor. A small flexible catheter is placed in your lower back by an anesthesiologist. Medication flows continuously to numb the lower half of your body.
I Very effective pain relief I You stay awake and aware I Can be adjusted anytime
II
May
lower
blood
pressure II May slow pushing phase II Limits mobility

I IV / Injectable Opioids Medications such as fentanyl or morphine can be given through an IV or by injection to take the edge off contractions. They don't eliminate pain completely but can help you rest between contractions.
• Short-acting — effects wear off in 1–2 hours
• May cause drowsiness, nausea, or dizziness
• Timing matters — avoided close to delivery to prevent
newborn breathing effects

I Local Anesthesia (Perineal Block) An injection directly into the perineal tissue, used at the time of delivery to numb the area for repair of a tear or episiotomy. It does not reduce contraction pain.

You can change your mind at any time. Choosing or declining an epidural early does not lock you in. Many people who plan unmedicated births choose an epidural once active labor begins — and that is completely fine. Likewise, an epidural can be given at almost any point before delivery.

I Talk to us before your due date about your preferences. We will share your birth preferences with the Labor & Delivery team. The goal is a safe, supported experience — whatever that looks like for you.

5a5495e0.subtitle: Understanding this birth complication.

blocks.text: Women's Specialists of Clear Lake
Dr. Geffrey H. Klein, MD · FACOG · DABOM · 400 W Medical Center Blvd, Suite 300, Webster, TX 77598 · (281) 557-0300
Shoulder Dystocia
A rare birth emergency where the baby's shoulder gets stuck -- our team is trained to respond quickly and safely
WHAT IS SHOULDER DYSTOCIA?
A condition during vaginal delivery when the baby's shoulder gets stuck behind the mother's pelvic bone after the head delivers
It is an obstetric emergency that requires quick, coordinated action by your delivery team
It is uncommon and most often resolved successfully with specific maneuvers
There are usually no warning symptoms for the mother -- it is recognized when the baby's shoulders do not deliver after the head
WHO IS AT HIGHER RISK?
Babies estimated to be larger than average (macrosomia)
Diabetes during pregnancy (gestational or pre-existing)
Excess maternal body weight or excessive pregnancy weight gain
A previous delivery complicated by shoulder dystocia
Prolonged second stage of labor or operative vaginal delivery
Important: Most cases happen with no risk factors at all -- it cannot be reliably predicted or always prevented
HOW WE TREAT IT
We will ask you to stop pushing for a moment so we can reposition
McRoberts maneuver: bringing your thighs up onto your belly to open the pelvis
Suprapubic pressure: gentle pressure just above the pubic bone to free the shoulder
Reaching into the vagina to rotate the baby or deliver the back arm
Other position changes (such as hands-and-knees) if needed
Most cases are resolved within a few minutes using these steps
POSSIBLE COMPLICATIONS
For baby: a fractured collarbone or arm bone -- usually heals well on its own
Brachial plexus injury (Erb's palsy): stretching of the nerves in the neck/shoulder causing arm weakness; most cases recover within weeks to months
Brief drop in baby's oxygen during the stuck period
For mother: vaginal or perineal tears, and heavier-than-usual bleeding
Our team will examine you and your baby carefully after delivery
REDUCING YOUR RISK
Manage blood sugar carefully if you have diabetes or gestational diabetes
Aim for healthy pregnancy weight gain as recommended at your visits
Stay active with provider-approved exercise during pregnancy
Attend all prenatal appointments so we can monitor baby's growth
Discuss any concerns about baby's size with your provider
PLANNING A FUTURE PREGNANCY
If you had shoulder dystocia before, the chance of recurrence is low but increased
We will review the details of the prior delivery -- baby's size, severity, any injury
A planned cesarean (C-section) may be recommended in some situations
Optimizing weight and blood sugar before pregnancy lowers your risk
We will create a personalized delivery plan with you
⚠AFTER DELIVERY -- CALL US IF YOU NOTICE
Heavy vaginal bleeding (soaking a pad in under an hour)
Severe pelvic, vaginal, or abdominal pain
Fever above 100.4 degrees F
Foul-smelling vaginal discharge
Baby is not moving an arm normally
Baby's arm appears limp or in an unusual position
Baby is not feeding well or seems unusually fussy
Any concern about you or your baby's recovery
You Are in Experienced Hands

Shoulder dystocia is uncommon, and our team trains regularly to respond safely and quickly when it does occur. Most babies and mothers recover fully with no lasting effects. If you have a history of shoulder dystocia, diabetes, or concerns about your baby's size, please talk with us -- together we will make a delivery plan that protects you and your baby.

🏁Signs of Labor
How to know when it's time to head to the hospital
What happens when labor begins
As labor begins, the cervix opens (dilates). The uterus, which contains muscle, contracts at regular intervals. When it contracts, the
abdomen becomes hard. Between the contractions, the uterus relaxes and becomes soft. Up to the start of labor and during early labor,
the baby will continue to move.
Certain changes also may signal that labor is beginning. You may or may not notice some of them before labor begins:
What is false labor?
Your uterus may contract o! and on before "true" labor begins. These irregular contractions are called false labor or Braxton Hicks
contractions. They are normal but can be painful at times. You might notice them more at the end of the day.
How can I tell the di!erence between true labor and false labor?
Usually, false labor contractions are less regular and not as strong as true labor. Sometimes the only way to tell the di!erence is by having
a vaginal exam to look for changes in your cervix that signal the onset of labor.
One good way to tell the di!erence is to time the contractions. Note how long it is from the start of one contraction to the start of the
next one. Keep a record for an hour. It may be hard to time labor pains accurately if the contractions are slight.
Please go to the hospital if:
your water breaks
you bleed like a period
your baby is not moving or not moving well
you have painful contractions 5 minutes apart for an hour

blocks.text: Women's Specialists of Clear Lake
Dr. Geffrey H. Klein, MD · FACOG · DABOM · 400 W Medical Center Blvd, Suite 300, Webster, TX 77598 · (281) 557-0300
VBAC: Vaginal Birth After Cesarean
If you have had a prior cesarean, you may have a choice -- a planned repeat cesarean or a trial of labor (TOLAC) toward a VBAC
WHAT IS VBAC AND TOLAC?
VBAC = a vaginal birth after a previous cesarean delivery
TOLAC = the trial of labor attempted in order to achieve a VBAC
If TOLAC is successful, you have a vaginal birth (a VBAC)
If TOLAC is not successful, you will have a repeat cesarean delivery
Most appropriate candidates with one prior low transverse cesarean have about a 60-80% chance of a successful VBAC
The decision is shared -- based on your history, this pregnancy, and your goals
BENEFITS OF A SUCCESSFUL VBAC
No abdominal surgery and no surgical scar from this birth
Shorter recovery -- usually back to normal activities sooner
Less blood loss than a cesarean
Lower risk of infection
Earlier bonding and breastfeeding start in many cases
Avoids risks of repeat cesareans -- bowel/bladder injury, hysterectomy, and placenta accreta or previa in future pregnancies
Especially valuable if you plan to have more children
RISKS TO KNOW ABOUT
Uterine rupture -- the prior scar opens during labor; rare (less than 1% with one low transverse scar) but serious for mom and baby
Failed TOLAC ending in cesarean -- carries higher infection and blood-loss risk than a planned repeat cesarean
Need for emergency cesarean, blood transfusion, or hysterectomy
Rare but possible: injury to the baby if rupture occurs
Risks are lower with: prior vaginal birth, spontaneous labor, one prior low-transverse incision
Risks are higher with: induction or augmentation of labor, short interval since last cesarean, more than one prior cesarean, large baby
WHY YOUR PRIOR INCISION MATTERS
The scar on your uterus is what matters -- not the scar on your skin (they can differ)
Low transverse (side-to-side, lower uterus) -- most common; lowest rupture risk; VBAC is an option
Low vertical (up-and-down, lower uterus) -- higher rupture risk; VBAC may still be considered case-by-case
Classical / high vertical (upper uterus, often used in very preterm cesareans) -- highest rupture risk; VBAC is NOT
recommended
Please request your operative report from any prior cesarean so we can review the exact incision type
If records are unavailable, we will discuss the safest plan based on your history
WHO IS A GOOD VBAC CANDIDATE?
One (sometimes two) prior low transverse cesarean(s)
No other uterine surgery with full-thickness incisions (eg, certain myomectomies)
No prior uterine rupture
Single baby, head-down, at term
No medical or obstetric reason that requires cesarean (eg, placenta previa)
Delivering at a hospital equipped for emergency cesarean with anesthesia and OR available 24/7
Spontaneous labor is ideal -- induction is sometimes possible but increases risk and lowers success rate
WHAT TO EXPECT IN LABOR
Continuous fetal heart-rate monitoring -- the most reliable early sign of uterine rupture
IV access placed on arrival in case of emergency
Epidural anesthesia is allowed and does not hide rupture symptoms
Avoid certain induction agents (eg, prostaglandins like misoprostol) due to higher rupture risk
Plans can change -- if labor stalls, the baby is in distress, or new risks appear, we may recommend cesarean
If you arrive in active labor when a repeat cesarean was planned, VBAC may still be safer at that point
Bring your birth preferences -- they help guide care, even if plans shift
⚠CALL OR GO TO LABOR & DELIVERY IMMEDIATELY FOR
Severe or sudden abdominal pain, especially between contractions
A 'tearing' or 'ripping' sensation in the abdomen
Vaginal bleeding heavier than spotting
Sudden change in contraction pattern or loss of contractions
Lightheadedness, fainting, or rapid heartbeat
Leaking fluid from the vagina (possible water breaking)
Any concern that something feels 'wrong' -- trust your instincts
Decreased or absent fetal movement
Your Birth, Your Choice -- With the Right Information

Both VBAC and a planned repeat cesarean are reasonable, safe options for the right candidate. There is no single 'right' answer -- the best choice depends on your medical history, this pregnancy, your future family plans, and what feels right to you. Bring your prior operative report (or let us help request it), your questions, and your birth goals to your prenatal visit. We will go through the numbers together and build a plan that puts you and your baby first.

Common Breastfeeding Problems
Most breastfeeding difficulties can be overcome with the right support — don't give up, and don't hesitate to ask for help
IS MY BABY GETTING ENOUGH MILK?
By day 5: at least 6–8 wet diapers and 3+ stools daily
Newborns feed 8–12 times per 24 hours; by 4 weeks, 7–9
times
Some weight loss is normal — up to 7% in the first 3–5 days
Baby should regain birth weight by 1–2 weeks of life
If baby seems hungrier than usual, it may be a growth spurt (2–4 weeks, 6 weeks, 3 and 6 months)
SORE & CRACKED NIPPLES
Most common cause: improper latch — correcting position usually fixes it
Mild sensitivity is normal the first week and resolves by day
Pain that persists or worsens throughout a feeding = nipple
injury
Apply antibiotic ointment (bacitracin/mupirocin) to cracked nipples with a nonstick pad
Lanolin is commonly used but evidence for benefit is limited
Check baby for tongue-tie if latch problems persist despite good technique
ENGORGEMENT & BLOCKED DUCTS
Engorgement (days 3–5): breasts feel full, firm, and tender as milk comes in
Hand-express a small amount before feeding to soften the areola for latch
Blocked ducts: tender lump without fever — feed on demand, avoid over-pumping
Use cold compresses between feeds and ibuprofen for pain/inflammation
Avoid deep massage or vibrating devices — they can worsen
inflammation
If not improved in 48 hours or fever develops, call your doctor (may be mastitis)
MASTITIS & BREAST INFECTIONS
Mastitis: red, painful, swollen area of breast, often with fever and flu-like symptoms
Most common in the first 3 months postpartum
Continue breastfeeding — stopping can make it worse
Antibiotics may be needed if symptoms don't improve in 24–
48 hours
A fluctuant, tender mass may indicate a breast abscess (needs drainage)
"Candidal" breast infections are often overdiagnosed — testing can confirm
LOW MILK SUPPLY
Most common fix: more frequent nursing with proper latch technique
Milk typically "comes in" by 72 hours — delayed in ~20% of women
Stress, obesity, diabetes, PCOS, and some medications can affect supply
Avoid unnecessary formula supplements — they can reduce milk production
Galactagogues (herbal or prescription) are not recommended — limited evidence
If supplementation is needed, use syringe/cup instead of bottle when possible
TIPS FOR SUCCESS
Get a lactation consultant evaluation early if you're struggling
Ensure baby's mouth is wide open with chin buried in breast during latch
Nurse in a comfortable position — try cradle, cross-cradle,
football, or side-lying
Most medications are safe while breastfeeding (check LactMed database)
Wean gradually — drop one session every 2–5 days to avoid engorgement
⚠CALL YOUR DOCTOR OR LACTATION CONSULTANT IF
Baby has lost more than 10% of birth weight
Fewer than 6 wet diapers per day after day 5
Nipple pain that worsens or persists beyond the first week
Breastfeeding Gets Easier — You're Doing a Great Job
Breast redness, swelling, or fever (possible mastitis)
Baby is not back to birth weight by 2 weeks of age
You feel overwhelmed, sad, or anxious about breastfeeding

Almost every breastfeeding challenge has a solution. With proper support and technique, most difficulties resolve within the first few weeks. You are not alone — our team and lactation consultants are here to help you every step of the way!

Women's Specialists of Clear Lake
Dr. Geffrey H. Klein, MD · FACOG · DABOM · 400 W Medical Center Blvd, Suite 300, Webster, TX 77598 · (281) 557-0300
🍼Circumcision
Understanding the procedure, benefits, risks, and aftercare for your newborn
WHAT IS CIRCUMCISION?

Circumcision is the surgical removal of the foreskin — the fold of skin covering the tip (glans) of the penis. It is one of the most commonly performed surgical procedures in the U.S., with approximately 60% of newborn males circumcised. The AAP states the benefits outweigh risks, but the decision is personal.
THE PROCEDURE
Performed in the hospital within 24–48 hrs of birth
Local anesthesia (dorsal penile nerve block) is used
Three common techniques: Gomco clamp, Plastibell, Mogen clamp
Takes 5–15 minutes
Healing takes 7–10 days
Sugar pacifier offered for comfort during procedure
BENEFITS VS. RISKS — AAP POSITION
✓ Potential Benefits
Lower risk of urinary tract infections (UTIs)
Lower risk of penile cancer (rare)
Reduced risk of some STIs (HIV, HPV, herpes)
Prevents phimosis (tight foreskin)
Easier genital hygiene
⚠ Potential Risks
Bleeding (most common complication, 1–2%)
Infection (rare with proper care)
Meatal stenosis (narrowing of urethral opening)
Unsatisfactory cosmetic result
Severe complications very rare (<0.2%)
AFTERCARE INSTRUCTIONS
Apply petrolatum (Vaseline) with each diaper change
Gently clean with warm water at each diaper change
Avoid soap on healing area for first week
If Plastibell used, ring falls off in 5–10 days
Yellow film (normal healing) — do not remove
Avoid wipes with fragrance/alcohol until healed
WHO SHOULD NOT BE CIRCUMCISED
Premature or unstable newborns
Hypospadias (urethral opening not at tip)
Chordee or other penile abnormalities
Family history of bleeding disorders
Ambiguous genitalia
Always deferred until baby is stable and healthy
⚠ CALL YOUR DOCTOR IF YOU NOTICE
Active bleeding that doesn't stop with pressure
Fever over 100.4°F in the newborn
Yellow-green discharge (not normal yellow film)
Plastibell ring still in place after 10 days
Swelling, redness, or pus at the site
Baby not urinating within 6–8 hours after procedure
Foul odor from the circumcision site
Extreme pain or prolonged crying after first day

💚 You Are Making the Best Choice for Your Family The decision to circumcise is personal and involves cultural, religious, and medical considerations. There is no universally right answer. Whatever you decide, your baby will be cared for with skill and compassion. If you proceed with circumcision, the procedure is safe, quick, and well-tolerated by newborns.

blocks.text: Postpartum Depression
Women's Specialists of Clear Lake
Dr. Geffrey H. Klein, MD · FACOG · DABOM · 400 W Medical Center Blvd, Suite 300, Webster, TX 77598 · (281) 557-0300
💜Postpartum Depression (PPD)
You are not alone — PPD is common, treatable, and not your fault
WHAT IS PPD?

Postpartum depression is a mood disorder affecting 1 in 5 new mothers. It is caused by the dramatic hormonal drop after delivery combined with sleep deprivation, physical recovery, and the emotional demands of new parenthood. PPD is a medical condition — not a character flaw or weakness.
BABY BLUES VS. PPD
Baby Blues — affects 70–80% of mothers; tearfulness, mood swings, anxiety starting day 2–3, resolves by 2 weeks
PPD — more severe, lasts >2 weeks, starts within 1 year of delivery, interferes with function
Postpartum Psychosis — rare emergency; hallucinations, confusion, call 911
SYMPTOMS OF PPD
Persistent sadness, emptiness, or hopelessness
Loss of interest in activities you enjoyed
Trouble bonding with your baby
Excessive worry or anxiety about baby's safety
Difficulty sleeping (even when baby sleeps)
Changes in appetite (eating too much or too little)
Feeling like a bad mother
Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby
RISK FACTORS
History of depression, anxiety, or bipolar disorder
PPD in a previous pregnancy
Lack of social support or partner support
Financial stress or relationship problems
Difficult or traumatic birth
NICU admission or infant health problems
History of thyroid disorder
Unplanned or unwanted pregnancy
TREATMENT — IT WORKS!
Therapy — CBT and interpersonal therapy are highly effective
SSRIs — sertraline (Zoloft), paroxetine — safe in breastfeeding RX
SNRIs — venlafaxine, duloxetine RX
Brexanolone (Zulresso) — IV infusion, FDA approved for PPD RX
Peer support groups (Postpartum Support International)
Sleep, self-care, accepting help from others
We screen using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) at your postpartum visits. Score of ≥10 triggers a care conversation.
HOW TO GET HELP
Tell your OB or midwife honestly about your feelings
Postpartum Support International: 1-800-944-4773
PSI Helpline: Text HOME to 741741
Ask your partner or a trusted person to call for you if needed
Seek help early — PPD responds well to treatment
🚨 SEEK IMMEDIATE HELP IF YOU HAVE THOUGHTS OF HARMING YOURSELF OR YOUR BABY

Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) · Text HOME to 741741 · Call 911 or go to your nearest ER. Postpartum psychosis is a medical emergency — symptoms include hallucinations, confusion, paranoia, or rapidly changing mood. Do not leave the mother alone. Call 911.
⚠ CALL YOUR DOCTOR IF YOU EXPERIENCE
Sadness or emptiness that won't go away after 2 weeks
Feeling like your baby would be better off without you
Not eating or caring for yourself
Rage, irritability, or anger that feels uncontrollable
Unable to sleep even when baby sleeps
Panic attacks or severe anxiety
Feeling disconnected from your baby
Baby Blues worsening rather than improving

💚 You Are a Wonderful Mother — Please Ask for Help Reaching out for help is one of the bravest and most loving things you can do for yourself and your baby. PPD is not a sign that you don't love your child — it's a medical condition that responds beautifully to treatment. You deserve to feel well. Let us help you get there.

blocks.text: ZURZUVAE®
(zuranolone)
A 14-Day Treatment for Postpartum Depression
Women's Specialists of Clear Lake · Geffrey H. Klein, MD, FACOG, DABOM · Patient Education · April 2026
What Is ZURZUVAE?

ZURZUVAE is a prescription medication used to treat postpartum depression (PPD) in adults. It is taken for 14 days only. After completing the 2-week course, no further dosing is required. Some patients may notice improvement in symptoms as early as Day 3, with continued improvement over the treatment course.
Who Is It For?
ZURZUVAE is approved for adults diagnosed with postpartum depression, including those whose symptoms began:
During the third trimester
Within 4 weeks after delivery
Your healthcare provider will determine if this medication is appropriate for you.
How Is It Taken?
Taken once daily in the evening
Continue for 14 days total
Take exactly as prescribed
If you miss a dose, follow your prescriber's instructions.
⚠ IMPORTANT: Driving Warning (Boxed Warning)
ZURZUVAE can cause sleepiness and slow reaction time.
Do not drive or operate heavy machinery for at least 12 hours after each dose
This restriction applies for the entire 14-day treatment period
You may not be able to tell if you are impaired
Plan ahead for childcare, transportation, and work responsibilities during treatment.
Common Side Effects
Sleepiness (somnolence)
Dizziness
Fatigue
Contact your healthcare provider if side effects are severe or concerning.
Diarrhea
Common cold symptoms
Urinary tract infection
CNS Depression
ZURZUVAE may cause:
Sleepiness or confusion
Dizziness or balance problems
Increased risk of falls
Tell your provider if you take alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids, or other sedating medications.
⚠ Suicidal Thoughts or Worsening Depression
Monitor for:
New or worsening depression
Suicidal thoughts
Unusual behavior changes
Seek medical attention immediately if these occur.
Continued on back →
⚠ Pregnancy and Birth Control
ZURZUVAE may cause harm to a developing fetus.
Use effective contraception during treatment and for 1 week after your last dose.
Tell your provider if you are pregnant or planning pregnancy.
A pregnancy registry is available for women exposed during pregnancy.
Breastfeeding
ZURZUVAE passes into breast milk in low amounts. Discuss with your provider:
Benefits of breastfeeding
Your need for treatment
Potential risks to your infant
Liver or Kidney Problems
If you have significant liver or kidney disease, your provider may prescribe a lower dose.
Abuse and Dependence
ZURZUVAE is a Schedule IV controlled substance. It has potential for misuse or dependence.
Take only as prescribed
Do not share your medication
☎ When to Call Your Provider
Contact your healthcare provider if you experience:
Severe drowsiness or confusion
Difficulty staying awake
Worsening mood
Thoughts of self-harm
Severe dizziness or falls
You Are Not Alone
Postpartum depression is common and treatable. ZURZUVAE offers a short, 14-day treatment option that may help relieve
symptoms quickly. If you have questions about whether this medication is right for you, please discuss them with your healthcare
provider.

Understanding Early Pregnancy
Loss
Miscarriage
What to expect, your options, and when to call — you are not alone
Patient Education · Obstetrics
400 W Medical Center Blvd, Ste 300 · Webster, TX 77598
❤ WHAT IS A MISCARRIAGE?
A Common Loss — Not Your Fault
Miscarriage is the loss of a pregnancy before 20 weeks. Most are caused by random chromosome problems — not by anything you did, ate, or lifted.
Common Symptoms
Vaginal bleeding and crampy lower-belly pain, sometimes with passage of clots or tissue. Pregnancy symptoms (nausea, breast tenderness) may fade.
Sometimes No Symptoms
A loss can be found on a routine ultrasound before any bleeding starts (a "missed" miscarriage).
Important: bleeding in early pregnancy is common and does not always mean a miscarriage. An ultrasound confirms the diagnosis.
🚨 YOUR MANAGEMENT OPTIONS
If you are stable, there is no emergency — you have time to decide. All three options are safe and effective; the choice is yours.
1 Expectant (natural): wait for the tissue to pass on its own. Good if you prefer no medicine or procedure and can wait.
2 Medication: pills (misoprostol, often with mifepristone) help your body pass the tissue on a more predictable timeline, usually at home.
3 Surgical (uterine aspiration): a short procedure that empties the uterus. Best for immediate, predictable completion or heavy bleeding.
We'll review the risks, benefits, and what to expect with each, and check your blood type — Rh-negative patients may need a RhoGAM injection.
🚨 WHAT TO EXPECT AT HOME
Bleeding & Cramping
Expect bleeding heavier than a period with cramping as tissue passes. This often peaks over a few hours, then eases.
Pain Relief
Ibuprofen (Advil/Motrin) works well for cramps. Use a heating pad and rest as needed.
Recovery
Light bleeding/spotting can last 1–2 weeks. We'll arrange follow-up to confirm the process is complete.
Use pads, not tampons, and avoid intercourse until bleeding stops and we've cleared you, to lower infection risk.
🚨 WHEN TO GET HELP NOW
Go to the ER / call us right away if:
911 Soaking 2+ maxi pads per hour for 2 hours in a row
911 Feeling dizzy, faint, or your heart is racing
911 Fever over 100.4°F (38°C) or shaking chills
911 Foul-smelling vaginal discharge
911 Severe belly pain not helped by medication
These can signal heavy bleeding or infection and need prompt treatment. When in doubt, call us or go to the ER — don't wait.
Caring for Your Heart, Too

Grief after a pregnancy loss is real, and everyone experiences it differently — there is no "right" way to feel or a set timeline. Be gentle with yourself, lean on people you trust, and know that a miscarriage does not mean you can't have a healthy pregnancy in the future. We're here to answer questions, support you, and plan next steps whenever you're ready. Call us anytime at (281) 557-0300.

Understanding Ectopic
Pregnancy
What it is, how it's found, and how it's treated
Needs Prompt Care
🩺 This is not your fault — an ectopic pregnancy can happen even with no known risk factors. Early diagnosis and treatment are the best ways to protect your health.
💊 WHAT IS AN ECTOPIC PREGNANCY?
Implants Outside the Uterus
Normally a fertilized egg grows inside the uterus. In an ectopic pregnancy it implants outside the main cavity — most often in a fallopian tube.
Why It's Serious A pregnancy outside the uterus cannot develop normally. As it grows it can cause internal bleeding and become life-threatening if untreated.
Common Symptoms (may be mild at first)
Vaginal spotting or bleeding Lower abdominal/pelvic pain, often on one side Cramping or low back pain Pain with bowel movements or urination
💊 CALL 911 / GO TO THE ER
Get emergency care right away for:
Sudden, severe, or worsening abdominal/pelvic pain
Shoulder pain, especially with weakness or dizziness
Fainting, feeling very lightheaded, or racing heartbeat
Heavy vaginal bleeding
Severe weakness, pale or clammy skin, feeling very unwell
These can be signs of internal bleeding from a ruptured ectopic pregnancy and need immediate care.
💊 HOW IS IT DIAGNOSED?

Pregnancy test — urine or blood test confirms pregnancy. Blood tests (hCG) — the pregnancy hormone is often checked twice, ~48 hours apart. The trend helps guide diagnosis but can't confirm ectopic by itself. Transvaginal ultrasound — a small probe looks closely at the uterus, tubes, and ovaries. Physical exam — checks for tenderness, bleeding, or signs of internal bleeding.
Sometimes it's too early to see on ultrasound (a "pregnancy of unknown location"). Repeat blood tests and ultrasounds are important until the location and outcome are clear.
💊 TREATMENT OPTIONS
Treatment depends on your symptoms, ultrasound, hCG levels, health, and pregnancy goals.

Close monitoring — if hCG is already low and falling, the body may resolve it on its own. Requires reliable follow-up blood tests. Methotrexate — an injection that stops the pregnancy from growing, if
unruptured and you're stable. Needs repeat hCG tests over weeks; some need another dose or surgery.
Surgery — for rupture, internal bleeding, or when medication isn't right. Usually laparoscopy; the tube may be preserved or removed.
Future Fertility & Emotional Support

Many people go on to have a healthy pregnancy after an ectopic pregnancy, though the risk of another is somewhat higher — in a future pregnancy, contact us early for hCG testing and an early ultrasound. This can also be emotionally hard; grief, sadness, and anxiety are common, and support from loved ones, counseling, or a pregnancy-loss group can help. Remember: a positive pregnancy test with pelvic/abdominal pain, bleeding, dizziness, or shoulder pain needs urgent evaluation. Call us anytime at (281) 557-0300.

💊Methotrexate for Ectopic Pregnancy
Treatment, follow-up, and recovery guide — what to expect during non-surgical ectopic pregnancy management
❓ WHAT IS AN ECTOPIC PREGNANCY?
An ectopic pregnancy occurs when a fertilized egg implants outside the uterus — most commonly in a fallopian tube. It cannot survive and must be treated promptly.
📊 Affects ~1 in 50 pregnancies (2%)
🏥 Medical emergency if tube ruptures — requires immediate surgery
🔬 Diagnosed with blood hCG levels and transvaginal ultrasound
✅ When caught early, methotrexate can treat it non-surgically
🚨 Seek immediate care if you have severe pelvic pain, shoulder tip pain, or
feeling faint — these may indicate rupture.
💉 HOW METHOTREXATE WORKS
🧬 Methotrexate is a medication that stops rapidly dividing cells (the developing pregnancy tissue) 💉 Given as a single IM injection (rarely split-dose)
📅 Most effective when hCG is <5,000 mIU/mL and no cardiac activity on ultrasound
⏰ Takes days to weeks for hCG to decline to zero
Who Is a Candidate?
✅ Hemodynamically stable (not in shock)
✅ Small ectopic (<3.5 cm), no rupture
✅ Able to follow up reliably for monitoring
✅ Normal liver, kidney, and bone marrow function
❌ Not for: rupture, heart activity present, very high hCG, or immunocompromised
📅 FOLLOW-UP SCHEDULE
After injection, your hCG must be monitored closely. You may see a temporary RISE in hCG days 1–4 — this is normal and does not mean treatment failure.
Blood draw for hCG — baseline post-injection level
Day 4
Second hCG — must drop ≥15% from Day 4 to confirm success
Day 7
Continue weekly hCG until level reaches zero (may take 4–6 weeks)
Weekly
⚠️ If hCG does NOT drop ≥15% by Day 7, a second dose or surgery may be required. Do not miss your lab appointments!
⚠️ RESTRICTIONS DURING TREATMENT
🚫 AVOID Until hCG = Zero:
Alcohol — increases liver toxicity risk
NO
Folic acid / prenatal vitamins — counteracts methotrexate
NO
NO
NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) — increases side effects
NO
Unprotected sex or attempts to conceive — wait at least 3 months after
hCG reaches zero
NO
Sun exposure without sunscreen — photosensitivity
NO
Strenuous activity — rupture risk
Common Side Effects (Usually Mild)
🤢 Nausea, vomiting, mouth sores
😔 Fatigue, mild abdominal cramping (Days 3–7)
📈 Temporary hCG rise (Days 1–4) — DO NOT PANIC
We Are With You Through This

An ectopic pregnancy is a loss, and it's okay to grieve. Methotrexate is highly effective when used in appropriate candidates — most women can go on to have successful pregnancies afterward. Please never hesitate to call us if you develop new or worsening pain, heavy bleeding, or feel unwell. Emergency line: (281) 557-0300 — available to you 24/7. 🧡

blocks.text: Understanding Your Treatment
Options for Ectopic Pregnancy
What Is an Ectopic Pregnancy?
An ectopic pregnancy occurs when a fertilized egg implants outside the uterus, most
commonly in a fallopian tube. Unfortunately, this type of pregnancy cannot continue and poses
serious health risks if untreated, including internal bleeding and damage to reproductive
organs.
Why Treatment Is Necessary
Without treatment, an ectopic pregnancy can rupture, causing life-threatening bleeding.
Prompt diagnosis and care are critical. Fortunately, there are safe and effective options to treat
it—medical management with methotrexate or surgical treatment.
Treatment Options
1. Medical Management: Methotrexate
What it is:
Methotrexate is a medication that stops cells from dividing and growing. It allows your body to
absorb the pregnancy tissue over time.
Who it's for:
Stable vital signs
No signs of rupture or internal bleeding
Low and declining pregnancy hormone levels (hCG)
Ectopic mass is small and unruptured
No contraindications to the drug (e.g. liver or kidney disease)
What to expect:
Given as a single or multiple intramuscular injections
Requires close follow-up with blood tests (hCG levels checked every few days to ensure
they’re dropping)
You may have cramping, spotting, or light bleeding
Avoid alcohol, NSAIDs (like ibuprofen), and folic acid supplements during treatment
Pros:
No surgery or anesthesia
Preserves the fallopian tube
Outpatient treatment
Cons:
Takes longer for full resolution
Requires frequent monitoring and follow-up
Possible side effects: nausea, fatigue, mouth sores, abdominal pain
May not work in all cases (5–20% may need a second dose or surgery)
2. Surgical Treatment
What it is:
Surgical removal of the ectopic pregnancy, typically done through laparoscopy (minimally
invasive surgery). In some cases, open surgery (laparotomy) may be necessary.
Types of surgery:
Salpingostomy: Removal of pregnancy tissue from the fallopian tube, leaving the tube intact
Salpingectomy: Removal of the entire affected fallopian tube (used if it’s severely damaged or
bleeding)
Who it's for:
Signs of internal bleeding or rupture
High or rising hCG levels
Contraindications to methotrexate
Failed medical therapy
Preference for a quicker resolution
What to expect:
General anesthesia is used
Usually performed as outpatient surgery
Recovery takes several days to a couple of weeks
Pros:
Quick resolution
Immediate removal of pregnancy
Option if medical therapy fails or isn’t safe
Cons:
Risks of surgery: bleeding, infection, injury to nearby organs
May reduce fertility if a tube is removed
Future Fertility Considerations
Most women can go on to have healthy pregnancies after treatment. Your provider may
recommend waiting 2–3 months before trying again after methotrexate, or until fully healed
after surgery. If one fallopian tube is removed, the other can still support pregnancy. Discuss
fertility concerns with your provider.
When to Seek Emergency Care
Go to the ER immediately if you have:
Severe abdominal or shoulder pain
Dizziness or fainting
Heavy vaginal bleeding
Rapid heartbeat
Final Thoughts
The choice between methotrexate and surgery depends on your specific condition, your
medical history, and your goals for future fertility. Your provider will guide you through the
safest and most appropriate option for you.
